O for a Muse of fire, that would ascend / The brightest heaven of invention, / A kingdom for a stage, princes to act, / And monarchs to behold the swelling scene! / Then should the warlike Harry, like himself, / Assume the port of Mars; and at his heels, / Leash'd in like hounds, should famine, sword, and fire / Crouch for employment. But pardon, gentles all, / The flat unraised spirits that hath dar'd / On this unworthy scaffold to bring forth / So great an object. Can this cockpit hold / The vasty fields of France? Or may we cram / Within this wooden O the very casques / That did affright the air at Agincourt? / O, pardon! since a crooked figure may / Attest in little place a million; / And let us, ciphers to this great accompt, / On your imaginary forces work. / Suppose within the girdle of these walls / Are now confin'd two mighty monarchies, / Whose high upreared and abutting fronts / The perilous narrow ocean parts asunder; / Piece out our imperfections with your thoughts: / Into a thousand parts divide one man, / And make imaginary puissance; / Think, when we talk of horses, that you see them / Printing their proud hoofs i' the receiving earth. / For 'tis your thoughts that now must deck our kings, / Carry them here and there, jumping o'er times, / Turning the accomplishment of many years / Into an hour-glass: for the which supply, / Admit me Chorus to this history; / Who, prologue-like, your humble patience pray, / Gently to hear, kindly to judge, our play.

If only we had a Muse of fire, able to climb to the brightest heaven of imagination: a whole kingdom for a stage, princes as actors, and kings to watch the swelling scene! Then warlike Harry, true to himself, would take on the bearing of Mars, god of war, and at his heels famine, sword and fire would crouch like leashed hounds, waiting to be let loose. But forgive us, gentle audience, for the dull, uninspired minds that have dared to bring so great a subject onto this unworthy platform. Can this cockpit of a theatre hold the vast fields of France? Can we cram into this wooden O even the helmets that frightened the very air at Agincourt? Oh, forgive us! Since a little zero added to a figure can stand for a million in a small space, let us, mere zeros beside this great sum, work on your imaginations. Imagine that within the circle of these walls two mighty kingdoms are now shut up, whose high, facing fronts are separated only by the dangerous narrow sea. Make up for our shortcomings with your thoughts. Divide one man into a thousand and create an imaginary army. When we talk of horses, picture them pressing their proud hooves into the soft earth. For it is your thoughts that must dress our kings now, carry them from place to place, leap over time, and squeeze the events of many years into an hour-glass. To help with that, let me be the Chorus to this history, and, like a prologue, humbly ask you to listen patiently and judge our play kindly.

My lord, I'll tell you: that self bill is urg'd, / Which in the eleventh year of the last king's reign / Was like, and had indeed against us pass'd, / But that the scambling and unquiet time / Did push it out of farther question.

My lord, I'll tell you: that very bill is being pushed again, the one that in the eleventh year of the last king's reign was likely to pass, and would have passed against us, if the disorder and unrest of the times had not pushed it out of further debate.
But how, my lord, shall we resist it now?
But how, my lord, are we going to resist it now?

It must be thought on. If it pass against us, / We lose the better half of our possession; / For all the temporal lands, which men devout / By testament have given to the Church, / Would they strip from us; being valu'd thus: / As much as would maintain, to the King's honour, / Full fifteen earls and fifteen hundred knights, / Six thousand and two hundred good esquires; / And, to relief of lazars and weak age, / Of indigent faint souls, past corporal toil, / A hundred almshouses right well suppli'd; / And to the coffers of the King beside, / A thousand pounds by the year. Thus runs the bill.

It needs thinking about. If it passes against us, we lose the better half of our property, because they would strip from us all the lands that devout men have left to the Church in their wills, valued like this: enough to keep, to the King's credit, fifteen earls and fifteen hundred knights, six thousand two hundred squires, and, to care for lepers and the old and needy who are past physical work, a hundred well-stocked almshouses; and on top of that a thousand pounds a year for the King's treasury. That's what the bill says.
That would take a big drink out of our wealth.
It would drink the cup and everything in it.
But how can we prevent it?
The King is full of grace and fair regard.
The King is gracious and well-intentioned.
And a true lover of the holy Church.
And a true lover of the holy Church.

The courses of his youth promis'd it not. / The breath no sooner left his father's body, / But that his wildness, mortifi'd in him, / Seem'd to die too; yea, at that very moment / Consideration like an angel came / And whipp'd the offending Adam out of him, / Leaving his body as a paradise / To envelope and contain celestial spirits. / Never was such a sudden scholar made; / Never came reformation in a flood / With such a heady currance, scouring faults; / Nor never Hydra-headed wilfulness / So soon did lose his seat, and all at once, / As in this king.

His behaviour as a youth did not promise it. But no sooner had the breath left his father's body than his wildness seemed to die too, killed off in him. Yes, at that very moment, reflection came like an angel and whipped the sinful Adam out of him, leaving his body like a paradise fit to hold heavenly spirits. There was never such a sudden scholar made. Reform never came in such a headlong flood, scouring away faults, and never did many-headed stubbornness, like the Hydra, lose its throne so quickly and all at once as in this king.
We are blessed in the change.
We are blessed by the change.

Hear him but reason in divinity, / And, all-admiring, with an inward wish / You would desire the King were made a prelate; / Hear him debate of commonwealth affairs, / You would say it hath been all in all his study; / List his discourse of war, and you shall hear / A fearful battle rend'red you in music; / Turn him to any cause of policy, / The Gordian knot of it he will unloose, / Familiar as his garter; that, when he speaks, / The air, a charter'd libertine, is still, / And the mute wonder lurketh in men's ears, / To steal his sweet and honey'd sentences; / So that the art and practic' part of life / Must be the mistress to this theoric: / Which is a wonder how his Grace should glean it, / Since his addiction was to courses vain, / His companies unletter'd, rude, and shallow, / His hours fill'd up with riots, banquets, sports, / And never noted in him any study, / Any retirement, any sequestration / From open haunts and popularity.

Just hear him reason about theology, and, full of admiration, you would secretly wish the King were a bishop. Hear him debate the affairs of state, and you would say he had studied nothing else. Listen to him talk about war, and you will hear a terrible battle turned into music. Give him any political problem, and he will untie its Gordian knot as easily as his garter. When he speaks, the air, free as a licensed libertine, falls still, and silent wonder waits in men's ears to catch his sweet, honeyed sentences. It must be that experience and practice of life taught him this theory. Which is a wonder, since how could his Grace have picked it up, when he was given to idle pursuits, his companions ignorant, rough and shallow, his hours filled with riots, feasts and games, and no one ever saw him study, or withdraw, or keep apart from public places and common people?

The strawberry grows underneath the nettle, / And wholesome berries thrive and ripen best / Neighbour'd by fruit of baser quality; / And so the Prince obscur'd his contemplation / Under the veil of wildness; which, no doubt, / Grew like the summer grass, fastest by night, / Unseen, yet crescive in his faculty.

The strawberry grows under the nettle, and good berries thrive and ripen best next to fruit of a lower kind. So the Prince hid his serious thoughts under a veil of wildness, and no doubt they grew like summer grass, fastest at night, unseen but steadily growing.
It must be so; for miracles are ceas'd, / And therefore we must needs admit the means / How things are perfected.
It must be so, because the age of miracles is over, so we have to accept that there are natural means by which things are made perfect.
But, my good lord, / How now for mitigation of this bill / Urg'd by the commons? Doth his Majesty / Incline to it, or no?
But, my good lord, what about softening this bill the Commons are pushing? Does his Majesty lean towards it or not?

He seems indifferent, / Or rather swaying more upon our part / Than cherishing the exhibiters against us; / For I have made an offer to his Majesty, / Upon our spiritual convocation / And in regard of causes now in hand, / Which I have open'd to his Grace at large, / As touching France, to give a greater sum / Than ever at one time the clergy yet / Did to his predecessors part withal.

He seems neutral, or rather leans more towards our side than towards those who brought it in against us. For I have made his Majesty an offer, on behalf of our church assembly and in view of the business now in hand, which I explained to him in full, concerning France: to give him a larger sum than the clergy have ever given at one time to any of his predecessors.
How did this offer seem receiv'd, my lord?
How did he seem to receive the offer, my lord?

With good acceptance of his Majesty; / Save that there was not time enough to hear, / As I perceiv'd his Grace would fain have done, / The severals and unhidden passages / Of his true titles to some certain dukedoms, / And generally to the crown and seat of France / Deriv'd from Edward, his great-grandfather.

His Majesty accepted it well, except that there wasn't time enough to hear, as I could see he wanted to, the details and clear line of descent of his true claim to certain dukedoms, and in general to the crown and throne of France, inherited from Edward the Third, his great-grandfather.
What was the impediment that broke this off?
The French ambassador upon that instant / Crav'd audience; and the hour, I think, is come / To give him hearing. Is it four o'clock?
The French ambassador asked for an audience at that moment, and I think the time has come to hear him. Is it four o'clock?
Then go we in, to know his embassy; / Which I could with a ready guess declare, / Before the Frenchman speak a word of it.
Then let's go in and hear his message, though I could guess it before the Frenchman says a word.
I'll wait upon you, and I long to hear it.
I'll come with you, and I'm eager to hear it.
Where is my gracious Lord of Canterbury?
Where is my gracious Lord of Canterbury?
Shall we call in the ambassador, my liege?
Shall we call in the ambassador, my lord?
Not yet, my cousin. We would be resolv'd, / Before we hear him, of some things of weight / That task our thoughts, concerning us and France.
Not yet, cousin. Before we hear him, we want to settle some weighty questions that occupy our thoughts about ourselves and France.
God and his angels guard your sacred throne / And make you long become it!
May God and his angels guard your sacred throne, and may you grace it for a long time!

Sure, we thank you. / My learned lord, we pray you to proceed / And justly and religiously unfold / Why the law Salique that they have in France / Or should, or should not, bar us in our claim; / And God forbid, my dear and faithful lord, / That you should fashion, wrest, or bow your reading, / Or nicely charge your understanding soul / With opening titles miscreate, whose right / Suits not in native colours with the truth; / For God doth know how many now in health / Shall drop their blood in approbation / Of what your reverence shall incite us to. / Therefore take heed how you impawn our person, / How you awake our sleeping sword of war. / We charge you, in the name of God, take heed; / For never two such kingdoms did contend / Without much fall of blood, whose guiltless drops / Are every one a woe, a sore complaint / 'Gainst him whose wrongs gives edge unto the swords / That makes such waste in brief mortality. / Under this conjuration speak, my lord; / For we will hear, note, and believe in heart / That what you speak is in your conscience wash'd / As pure as sin with baptism.

Thank you, truly. My learned lord, please go on and explain fairly and devoutly whether the Salic law they have in France ought or ought not to bar us in our claim. And God forbid, my dear and faithful lord, that you should twist, distort or bend your reading, or burden your conscience with subtle arguments for a false title that does not, in its true colours, match the truth. For God knows how many men now healthy will shed their blood to prove whatever your reverence urges us to do. So take care how you commit our person, how you wake our sleeping sword of war. We order you, in God's name, take care. For never did two such kingdoms fight without great bloodshed, and every innocent drop is a grief, a bitter accusation against the man whose wrongs sharpen the swords that waste so many short lives. Speak under this solemn charge, my lord, and we will listen, take note, and believe in our heart that what you say is washed as clean in your conscience as sin is in baptism.

Then hear me, gracious sovereign, and you peers, / That owe yourselves, your lives, and services / To this imperial throne. There is no bar / To make against your Highness' claim to France / But this, which they produce from Pharamond: / "In terram Salicam mulieres ne succedant," / "No woman shall succeed in Salique land;" / Which Salique land the French unjustly gloze / To be the realm of France, and Pharamond / The founder of this law and female bar. / Yet their own authors faithfully affirm / That the land Salique is in Germany, / Between the floods of Sala and of Elbe; / Where Charles the Great, having subdu'd the Saxons, / There left behind and settled certain French; / Who, holding in disdain the German women / For some dishonest manners of their life, / Establish'd then this law, to wit, no female / Should be inheritrix in Salique land; / Which Salique, as I said, 'twixt Elbe and Sala, / Is at this day in Germany call'd Meisen. / Then doth it well appear the Salique law / Was not devised for the realm of France; / Nor did the French possess the Salique land / Until four hundred one and twenty years / After defunction of King Pharamond, / Idly suppos'd the founder of this law, / Who died within the year of our redemption / Four hundred twenty-six; and Charles the Great / Subdu'd the Saxons, and did seat the French / Beyond the river Sala, in the year / Eight hundred five. Besides, their writers say, / King Pepin, which deposed Childeric, / Did, as heir general, being descended / Of Blithild, which was daughter to King Clothair, / Make claim and title to the crown of France. / Hugh Capet also, who usurp'd the crown / Of Charles the Duke of Lorraine, sole heir male / Of the true line and stock of Charles the Great, / To find his title with some shows of truth, / Though, in pure truth, it was corrupt and naught, / Convey'd himself as the heir to the Lady Lingare, / Daughter to Charlemain, who was the son / To Lewis the Emperor, and Lewis the son / Of Charles the Great. Also, King Lewis the Tenth, / Who was sole heir to the usurper Capet, / Could not keep quiet in his conscience, / Wearing the crown of France, till satisfied / That fair Queen Isabel, his grandmother, / Was lineal of the Lady Ermengare, / Daughter to Charles, the foresaid Duke of Lorraine; / By the which marriage the line of Charles the Great / Was re-united to the crown of France. / So that, as clear as is the summer's sun, / King Pepin's title and Hugh Capet's claim, / King Lewis his satisfaction, all appear / To hold in right and title of the female. / So do the kings of France unto this day, / Howbeit they would hold up this Salique law / To bar your Highness claiming from the female, / And rather choose to hide them in a net / Than amply to imbar their crooked titles / Usurp'd from you and your progenitors.

Then hear me, gracious king, and you lords who owe your selves, lives and service to this royal throne. There is no obstacle to your Highness's claim to France except this, which they quote from King Pharamond: "In terram Salicam mulieres ne succedant", "No woman shall inherit in Salic land". The French wrongly interpret this Salic land as the kingdom of France, and Pharamond as the founder of this law that bars women. Yet their own historians honestly state that the Salic land is in Germany, between the rivers Saale and Elbe, where Charlemagne, after conquering the Saxons, left some Frenchmen settled. They despised the German women for their loose way of life, and so made this law that no woman should inherit in Salic land. That Salic land, as I said, between the Elbe and the Saale, is now called Meissen in Germany. So it is clear the Salic law was not made for the kingdom of France. And the French did not hold the Salic land until four hundred and twenty-one years after the death of King Pharamond, wrongly supposed the founder of this law, who died in the year of our Lord 426; and Charlemagne conquered the Saxons and settled the French beyond the river Saale in the year 805. Besides, their writers say that King Pepin, who deposed Childeric, claimed the crown of France as general heir, because he was descended from Blithild, daughter of King Clothair. Hugh Capet, too, who seized the crown from Charles, Duke of Lorraine, the only male heir of Charlemagne's true line, tried to give his title some show of truth, though in fact it was corrupt and worthless, by presenting himself as heir to Lady Lingare, daughter of Charlemain, who was son of the Emperor Louis, who was son of Charlemagne. Also King Louis the Tenth, who was sole heir of the usurper Capet, could not rest easy in his conscience wearing the crown of France until he was satisfied that his grandmother, fair Queen Isabel, descended from Lady Ermengare, daughter of that same Charles, Duke of Lorraine. By that marriage Charlemagne's line was joined to the crown of France again. So, as clear as the summer sun, King Pepin's title, Hugh Capet's claim and King Louis's peace of mind all rest on descent through the female line. The kings of France do the same to this day, though they would hold up this Salic law to bar your Highness from claiming through the female, preferring to hide in a tangle of excuses rather than openly expose their crooked titles, stolen from you and your ancestors.
May I with right and conscience make this claim?
May I make this claim rightfully and with a clear conscience?

The sin upon my head, dread sovereign! / For in the book of Numbers is it writ, / When the man dies, let the inheritance / Descend unto the daughter. Gracious lord, / Stand for your own! Unwind your bloody flag! / Look back into your mighty ancestors! / Go, my dread lord, to your great-grandsire's tomb, / From whom you claim; invoke his warlike spirit, / And your great-uncle's, Edward the Black Prince, / Who on the French ground play'd a tragedy, / Making defeat on the full power of France, / Whiles his most mighty father on a hill / Stood smiling to behold his lion's whelp / Forage in blood of French nobility. / O noble English, that could entertain / With half their forces the full pride of France / And let another half stand laughing by, / All out of work and cold for action!

Let the sin be on my head, dread king! For in the Book of Numbers it is written: when a man dies, let his inheritance pass to his daughter. Gracious lord, stand up for what is yours! Unfurl your bloody battle flag! Look back to your mighty ancestors! Go, my dread lord, to the tomb of your great-grandfather, from whom you claim; call up his warlike spirit, and that of your great-uncle Edward the Black Prince, who staged a tragedy on French soil, defeating the whole army of France, while his mighty father stood smiling on a hill to watch his lion's cub feed on the blood of French nobles. Oh, those noble English, who could take on the full pride of France with half their forces, while the other half stood by laughing, idle and cold for want of action!

Awake remembrance of these valiant dead, / And with your puissant arm renew their feats. / You are their heir; you sit upon their throne; / The blood and courage that renowned them / Runs in your veins; and my thrice-puissant liege / Is in the very May-morn of his youth, / Ripe for exploits and mighty enterprises.

Bring back the memory of these brave dead men, and with your powerful arm repeat their deeds. You are their heir; you sit on their throne; the blood and courage that made them famous runs in your veins; and my mighty king is in the May morning of his youth, ripe for great exploits and enterprises.
Your brother kings and monarchs of the earth / Do all expect that you should rouse yourself, / As did the former lions of your blood.
Your fellow kings and rulers of the earth all expect you to rouse yourself as the earlier lions of your family did.

They know your Grace hath cause and means and might; / So hath your Highness. Never King of England / Had nobles richer, and more loyal subjects, / Whose hearts have left their bodies here in England / And lie pavilion'd in the fields of France.

They know your Grace has the cause, the means and the strength, and so you have. No King of England ever had richer nobles or more loyal subjects, whose hearts have already left their bodies here in England and are camped in tents in the fields of France.

O, let their bodies follow, my dear liege, / With blood and sword and fire to win your right; / In aid whereof we of the spiritualty / Will raise your Highness such a mighty sum / As never did the clergy at one time / Bring in to any of your ancestors.

Oh, let their bodies follow, my dear lord, with blood, sword and fire to win your right. To help with it, we of the clergy will raise your Highness a greater sum than the clergy ever brought to any of your ancestors at one time.
We must not only arm to invade the French, / But lay down our proportions to defend / Against the Scot, who will make road upon us / With all advantages.
We must not only arm to invade the French, but also set aside forces to defend ourselves against the Scots, who will raid us whenever they have the chance.
They of those marches, gracious sovereign, / Shall be a wall sufficient to defend / Our inland from the pilfering borderers.
The people of the border country, gracious king, will be wall enough to defend our heartland against thieving raiders.

We do not mean the coursing snatchers only, / But fear the main intendment of the Scot, / Who hath been still a giddy neighbour to us; / For you shall read that my great-grandfather / Never went with his forces into France / But that the Scot on his unfurnish'd kingdom / Came pouring, like the tide into a breach, / With ample and brim fullness of his force, / Galling the gleaned land with hot assays, / Girdling with grievous siege castles and towns; / That England, being empty of defence, / Hath shook and trembled at the ill neighbourhood.

We don't mean only the hit-and-run raiders; we fear a full invasion by the Scots, who have always been an unreliable neighbour to us. For you will read that my great-grandfather never took his forces into France without the Scots pouring into his undefended kingdom like the tide through a gap in a sea wall, in full force, harrying the stripped land with fierce attacks and surrounding castles and towns with cruel sieges, so that England, empty of defenders, shook and trembled at such a bad neighbour.

She hath been then more fear'd than harm'd, my liege; / For hear her but exampl'd by herself: / When all her chivalry hath been in France, / And she a mourning widow of her nobles, / She hath herself not only well defended / But taken and impounded as a stray / The King of Scots; whom she did send to France / To fill King Edward's fame with prisoner kings, / And make her chronicle as rich with praise / As is the ooze and bottom of the sea / With sunken wreck and sumless treasuries.

Then she was more frightened than hurt, my lord. Just take her own past as an example: when all her knights were in France and she was a widow mourning her absent nobles, she not only defended herself well but captured the King of Scots like a stray animal and sent him to France, to add captive kings to King Edward's fame, and to make her history as rich with praise as the ooze at the bottom of the sea is with sunken wrecks and countless treasure.

But there's a saying very old and true, / "If that you will France win, / Then with Scotland first begin." / For once the eagle England being in prey, / To her unguarded nest the weasel Scot / Comes sneaking and so sucks her princely eggs, / Playing the mouse in absence of the cat, / To tear and havoc more than she can eat.

But there's an old and true saying: "If you want to win France, start with Scotland." For once England, the eagle, is out hunting, the weasel Scot comes creeping to her unguarded nest and sucks her royal eggs, playing the mouse while the cat is away, and ruining more than she can eat.

It follows then the cat must stay at home; / Yet that is but a crush'd necessity, / Since we have locks to safeguard necessaries, / And pretty traps to catch the petty thieves. / While that the armed hand doth fight abroad, / The advised head defends itself at home; / For government, though high and low and lower, / Put into parts, doth keep in one consent, / Congreeing in a full and natural close, / Like music.

So it follows that the cat must stay at home. But that is a forced conclusion, since we have locks to protect our goods and clever traps to catch petty thieves. While the armed hand fights abroad, the wise head defends itself at home. For government, though made of high, low and lower ranks, each with its part, keeps in harmony, coming together in one full and natural ending, like music.

Therefore doth heaven divide / The state of man in divers functions, / Setting endeavour in continual motion, / To which is fixed, as an aim or butt, / Obedience; for so work the honey-bees, / Creatures that by a rule in nature teach / The act of order to a peopled kingdom. / They have a king and officers of sorts, / Where some, like magistrates, correct at home, / Others like merchants, venture trade abroad, / Others, like soldiers, armed in their stings, / Make boot upon the summer's velvet buds, / Which pillage they with merry march bring home / To the tent-royal of their emperor; / Who, busied in his majesty, surveys / The singing masons building roofs of gold, / The civil citizens kneading up the honey, / The poor mechanic porters crowding in / Their heavy burdens at his narrow gate, / The sad-eyed justice, with his surly hum, / Delivering o'er to executors pale / The lazy yawning drone. I this infer, / That many things, having full reference / To one consent, may work contrariously. / As many arrows, loosed several ways, / Come to one mark; as many ways meet in one town; / As many fresh streams meet in one salt sea; / As many lines close in the dial's centre; / So many a thousand actions, once afoot, / End in one purpose, and be all well borne / Without defeat. Therefore to France, my liege! / Divide your happy England into four, / Whereof take you one quarter into France, / And you withal shall make all Gallia shake. / If we, with thrice such powers left at home, / Cannot defend our own doors from the dog, / Let us be worried and our nation lose / The name of hardiness and policy.

That is why heaven divides human society into different roles, keeping effort always in motion, with obedience fixed as its aim or target. That is how honey-bees work, creatures that by natural law teach a populated kingdom how to be orderly. They have a king and officers of different ranks: some, like magistrates, keep order at home; others, like merchants, trade abroad; others, like soldiers armed with their stings, raid the soft buds of summer and bring the plunder home in merry procession to the royal tent of their emperor. He, busy with his royal duties, watches the singing masons building roofs of gold, the orderly citizens kneading the honey, the poor labourers crowding their heavy loads through his narrow gate, and the grave-eyed judge, with his stern hum, handing the lazy, yawning drone over to the pale executioners. From this I conclude: that many things, all directed to one agreed end, may work in different ways: as many arrows shot from different places hit one target, as many roads meet in one town, as many fresh streams flow into one salt sea, as many lines meet at the centre of a sundial, so a thousand actions, once begun, can end in one purpose and all succeed without failure. So, to France, my lord! Divide your fortunate England into four, take one quarter into France, and with it you will make all France shake. If we, with three times that many left at home, can't defend our own doors from the dog, let us be savaged, and let our nation lose its name for courage and good government.
Call in the messengers sent from the Dauphin.
Call in the messengers sent from the Dauphin.

Now are we well resolv'd; and, by God's help, / And yours, the noble sinews of our power, / France being ours, we'll bend it to our awe, / Or break it all to pieces. Or there we'll sit, / Ruling in large and ample empery / O'er France and all her almost kingly dukedoms, / Or lay these bones in an unworthy urn, / Tombless, with no remembrance over them. / Either our history shall with full mouth / Speak freely of our acts, or else our grave, / Like Turkish mute, shall have a tongueless mouth, / Not worshipp'd with a waxen epitaph.

Now we have made up our mind, and, with God's help and yours, the noble muscles of our power, since France is ours, we'll bend it to our authority or break it all to pieces. Either we'll sit there ruling in wide, full command over France and its almost royal dukedoms, or lay these bones in a humble urn, with no tomb and no memorial over them. Either our history will speak loudly and freely of our deeds, or else our grave, like a Turkish mute with his tongue cut out, will have no voice and not even the honour of a wax epitaph.
Now are we well prepar'd to know the pleasure / Of our fair cousin Dauphin; for we hear / Your greeting is from him, not from the King.
Now we are ready to hear what our fair cousin the Dauphin wants, since we hear your greeting is from him and not from the King.
May't please your Majesty to give us leave / Freely to render what we have in charge, / Or shall we sparingly show you far off / The Dauphin's meaning and our embassy?
Will your Majesty give us permission to speak our message freely, or should we just hint at the Dauphin's meaning and our mission from a distance?

We are no tyrant, but a Christian king, / Unto whose grace our passion is as subject / As is our wretches fett'red in our prisons; / Therefore with frank and with uncurbed plainness / Tell us the Dauphin's mind.
We are no tyrant but a Christian king, whose passion is as much ruled by our self-control as the wretches chained in our prisons. So tell us the Dauphin's mind openly and plainly.

Thus, then, in few. / Your Highness, lately sending into France, / Did claim some certain dukedoms, in the right / Of your great predecessor, King Edward the Third. / In answer of which claim, the prince our master / Says that you savour too much of your youth, / And bids you be advis'd there's nought in France / That can be with a nimble galliard won. / You cannot revel into dukedoms there. / He therefore sends you, meeter for your spirit, / This tun of treasure; and, in lieu of this, / Desires you let the dukedoms that you claim / Hear no more of you. This the Dauphin speaks.

Then, in brief: your Highness recently sent to France claiming certain dukedoms by right of your great ancestor King Edward the Third. In answer, the prince our master says that you smack too much of your youth, and advises you that nothing in France can be won by dancing a lively galliard; you cannot party your way into dukedoms there. So he sends you this barrel of treasure, more suitable to your character, and in return asks that the dukedoms you claim hear no more from you. That is the Dauphin's message.

We are glad the Dauphin is so pleasant with us. / His present and your pains we thank you for. / When we have match'd our rackets to these balls, / We will, in France, by God's grace, play a set / Shall strike his father's crown into the hazard. / Tell him he hath made a match with such a wrangler / That all the courts of France will be disturb'd / With chaces. And we understand him well, / How he comes o'er us with our wilder days, / Not measuring what use we made of them. / We never valu'd this poor seat of England; / And therefore, living hence, did give ourself / To barbarous licence; as 'tis ever common / That men are merriest when they are from home. / But tell the Dauphin I will keep my state, / Be like a king, and show my sail of greatness / When I do rouse me in my throne of France. / For that I have laid by my majesty / And plodded like a man for working days, / But I will rise there with so full a glory / That I will dazzle all the eyes of France, / Yea, strike the Dauphin blind to look on us. / And tell the pleasant prince this mock of his / Hath turn'd his balls to gun-stones, and his soul / Shall stand sore charged for the wasteful vengeance / That shall fly with them; for many a thousand widows / Shall this his mock mock out of their dear husbands, / Mock mothers from their sons, mock castles down; / And some are yet ungotten and unborn / That shall have cause to curse the Dauphin's scorn. / But this lies all within the will of God, / To whom I do appeal; and in whose name / Tell you the Dauphin I am coming on / To venge me as I may, and to put forth / My rightful hand in a well-hallow'd cause. / So get you hence in peace; and tell the Dauphin / His jest will savour but of shallow wit, / When thousands weep more than did laugh at it.-- / Convey them with safe conduct.--Fare you well.

We are glad the Dauphin is so playful with us. We thank you for his present and your trouble. When we have matched our rackets to these balls, we will, by God's grace, play a set in France that will knock his father's crown into the hazard. Tell him he has made a match with such a tough opponent that all the courts of France will be disturbed with chases. And we understand him well, how he taunts us with our wilder days, without measuring what use we made of them. We never valued this humble throne of England, and so, living away from it, we gave ourselves up to wild freedom, as men are always merriest when they are away from home. But tell the Dauphin I will keep my royal dignity, behave like a king, and show the full sail of my greatness when I rise up on my throne of France. For that I have set aside my majesty and plodded like a common working man; but I will rise there in such full glory that I will dazzle every eye in France, yes, strike the Dauphin blind to look at us. And tell the playful prince that his joke has turned his balls into cannonballs, and his soul will carry the heavy guilt for the destructive vengeance that flies with them. This mockery of his will mock many thousand widows out of their dear husbands, mock mothers out of their sons, mock castles down; and some not yet conceived or born will have reason to curse the Dauphin's scorn. But all this lies in the will of God, to whom I appeal, and in whose name tell the Dauphin I am coming to avenge myself as I can, and to stretch out my rightful hand in a holy cause. So go in peace, and tell the Dauphin his joke will seem shallow when thousands weep for it, more than ever laughed at it. (To attendants) Escort them safely. (To the Ambassadors) Farewell.

We hope to make the sender blush at it. / Therefore, my lords, omit no happy hour / That may give furtherance to our expedition; / For we have now no thought in us but France, / Save those to God, that run before our business. / Therefore, let our proportions for these wars / Be soon collected, and all things thought upon / That may with reasonable swiftness add / More feathers to our wings; for, God before, / We'll chide this Dauphin at his father's door. / Therefore let every man now task his thought, / That this fair action may on foot be brought.

We hope to make the sender blush for it. So, my lords, waste no good moment that could speed our expedition, for we now have no thought except France, apart from our thoughts of God, which come before our business. So let our supplies for these wars be gathered quickly, and everything considered that might sensibly add feathers to our wings; for, with God leading, we'll scold this Dauphin at his father's door. So let every man now put his mind to it, so that this good enterprise may be set in motion.

Now all the youth of England are on fire, / And silken dalliance in the wardrobe lies. / Now thrive the armourers, and honour's thought / Reigns solely in the breast of every man. / They sell the pasture now to buy the horse, / Following the mirror of all Christian kings, / With winged heels, as English Mercuries. / For now sits Expectation in the air, / And hides a sword from hilts unto the point / With crowns imperial, crowns, and coronets, / Promis'd to Harry and his followers. / The French, advis'd by good intelligence / Of this most dreadful preparation, / Shake in their fear, and with pale policy / Seek to divert the English purposes. / O England! model to thy inward greatness, / Like little body with a mighty heart, / What mightst thou do, that honour would thee do, / Were all thy children kind and natural! / But see thy fault! France hath in thee found out / A nest of hollow bosoms, which he fills / With treacherous crowns; and three corrupted men, / One, Richard Earl of Cambridge, and the second, / Henry Lord Scroop of Masham, and the third, / Sir Thomas Grey, knight of Northumberland, / Have, for the gilt of France,--O guilt indeed!-- / Confirm'd conspiracy with fearful France; / And by their hands this grace of kings must die, / If hell and treason hold their promises, / Ere he take ship for France, and in Southampton. / Linger your patience on, and we'll digest / The abuse of distance, force a play. / The sum is paid; the traitors are agreed; / The King is set from London; and the scene / Is now transported, gentles, to Southampton. / There is the playhouse now, there must you sit; / And thence to France shall we convey you safe, / And bring you back, charming the narrow seas / To give you gentle pass; for, if we may, / We'll not offend one stomach with our play. / But, till the King come forth, and not till then, / Unto Southampton do we shift our scene.

Now all the young men of England are on fire, and silk party clothes are left in the wardrobe. Now armourers do good business, and the thought of honour rules alone in every man's heart. They sell their pasture land to buy a horse, following the model of all Christian kings, with winged heels, like English versions of Mercury. For Expectation now sits in the air and hides a sword from hilt to point with crowns of kings, crowns and coronets, promised to Harry and his followers. The French, well informed by their spies about this terrible preparation, shake with fear and with pale cunning try to turn the English from their purpose. Oh England! You are a small model of your inner greatness, like a little body with a mighty heart. What might you not do that honour would have you do, if all your children were loving and loyal! But see your fault! France has found in you a nest of hollow hearts, which it fills with treacherous gold coins; and three corrupted men, first, Richard Earl of Cambridge, second, Henry Lord Scroop of Masham, and third, Sir Thomas Grey, knight of Northumberland, have, for the gilt of France (oh, guilt indeed!), sealed a conspiracy with frightened France; and by their hands this finest of kings must die, if hell and treason keep their promises, before he takes ship for France, in Southampton. Keep your patience a little longer, and we'll make you swallow the jumps in place and force them into a play. The bribe is paid, the traitors have agreed, the King has left London, and the scene now moves, gentlemen, to Southampton. That is the playhouse now, there you must sit, and from there we'll carry you safely to France and back, charming the narrow sea to give you a smooth crossing, for, if we can help it, we won't make a single stomach seasick with our play. But not until the King comes out, and not until then, will we shift our scene to Southampton.
What, are Ancient Pistol and you friends yet?
Well, are Ensign Pistol and you friends yet?

For my part, I care not. I say little; but when time shall / serve, there shall be smiles; but that shall be as it may. I dare / not fight, but I will wink and hold out mine iron. It is a simple / one, but what though? It will toast cheese, and it will endure / cold as another man's sword will; and there's an end.

As far as I'm concerned, I don't care. I say little, but when the time comes there shall be smiles; but that shall be as it may. I don't dare fight, but I'll shut my eyes and hold out my sword. It's a plain one, but so what? It will toast cheese, and it will stand the cold as well as any man's sword; and that's the end of it.
I will bestow a breakfast to make you friends; and we'll / be all three sworn brothers to France. Let it be so, good / Corporal Nym.
I'll pay for a breakfast to make you friends, and we'll all three be sworn brothers going to France. Let it be so, good Corporal Nym.
Faith, I will live so long as I may, that's the certain of it; and / when I cannot live any longer, I will do as I may. That is my rest, / that is the rendezvous of it.
Honestly, I'll live as long as I can, that's certain; and when I can't live any longer, I'll do as I can. That's my last word, that's the end of it.
It is certain, corporal, that he is married to Nell Quickly; and / certainly she did you wrong, for you were troth-plight to her.
It's certain, corporal, that he's married Nell Quickly; and she certainly wronged you, because you were engaged to her.

I cannot tell. Things must be as they may. Men may sleep, and / they may have their throats about them at that time; and some say / knives have edges. It must be as it may. Though patience be a / tired mare, yet she will plod. There must be conclusions. Well, I / cannot tell.

I can't say. Things must be as they may. Men may sleep, and they may have their throats with them at the time; and some say knives have edges. It must be as it may. Though patience is a tired old mare, she still plods on. There must be an end. Well, I can't say.
Here comes Ancient Pistol and his wife. Good Corporal, be / patient here. How now, mine host Pistol!
Here comes Ensign Pistol and his wife. Good Corporal, keep your temper here. Hello there, landlord Pistol!
Base tike, call'st thou me host? / Now, by this hand, I swear I scorn the term; / Nor shall my Nell keep lodgers.
Low mongrel, are you calling me landlord? By this hand, I swear I scorn the word, and my Nell won't keep lodgers either.

No, by my troth, not long; for we cannot lodge and board a / dozen or fourteen gentlewomen that live honestly by the prick of / their needles, but it will be thought we keep a bawdy house / straight. [Nym and Pistol draw] O well a day, Lady, if he be not / drawn now! We shall see wilful adultery and murder committed.

No, honestly, not for long; because we can't give room and board to twelve or fourteen respectable ladies who live honestly by sewing without people at once thinking we keep a brothel. (Nym and Pistol draw their swords) Oh dear, by Our Lady, he's drawn his sword! We'll see deliberate adultery and murder done here.
Good Lieutenant! good corporal! offer nothing here.
Good Lieutenant! Good Corporal! Don't start anything here.
Pish for thee, Iceland dog! thou prick-ear'd cur of Iceland!
Pish to you, you Iceland lapdog! You prick-eared cur from Iceland!
Good Corporal Nym, show thy valour, and put up your sword.
Good Corporal Nym, show how brave you are and put your sword away.
Will you shog off? I would have you solus.
Will you clear off? I want you alone.

"Solus," egregious dog! O viper vile! / The "solus" in thy most mervailous face; / The "solus" in thy teeth, and in thy throat, / And in thy hateful lungs, yea, in thy maw, perdy, / And, which is worse, within thy nasty mouth! / I do retort the "solus" in thy bowels; / For I can take, and Pistol's cock is up, / And flashing fire will follow.

"Alone", you outrageous dog! Oh vile viper! I throw "alone" in your most astonishing face, in your teeth and in your throat, in your hateful lungs, yes, in your belly, by God, and, what's worse, in your nasty mouth! I hurl "alone" back into your guts; for I can strike, and Pistol's cock is raised, and flashing fire will follow.

I am not Barbason; you cannot conjure me. I have an humour to / knock you indifferently well. If you grow foul with me, Pistol, I / will scour you with my rapier, as I may, in fair terms. If you / would walk off, I would prick your guts a little, in good terms, / as I may; and that's the humour of it.

I'm not the devil Barbason; you can't drive me off with spells. I have a mind to beat you fairly well. If you get nasty with me, Pistol, I'll clean you out with my rapier, as I may, in fair terms. If you'll walk off with me, I'll prick your guts a little, in good terms, as I may; and that's the humour of it.
O braggart vile and damned furious wight! / The grave doth gape, and doting death is near, / Therefore exhale.
Oh vile braggart and damned furious creature! The grave is gaping, and doting death is near; so breathe your last.
Hear me, hear me what I say. He that strikes the first / stroke I'll run him up to the hilts, as I am a soldier.
Listen to me, listen to what I say. Whoever strikes the first blow, I'll run him through up to the hilt, as I'm a soldier.
An oath of mickle might; and fury shall abate. / Give me thy fist, thy fore-foot to me give. / Thy spirits are most tall.
An oath of great power; and fury shall calm down. Give me your fist, give me your front paw. Your spirit is very brave.
I will cut thy throat, one time or other, in fair terms: / that is the humour of it.
I'll cut your throat some time or other, in fair terms; that's the humour of it.

"Couple a gorge!" / That is the word. I thee defy again. / O hound of Crete, think'st thou my spouse to get? / No! to the spital go, / And from the powdering tub of infamy / Fetch forth the lazar kite of Cressid's kind, / Doll Tearsheet she by name, and her espouse. / I have, and I will hold, the quondam Quickly / For the only she; and--pauca, there's enough. / Go to.

"Coupe la gorge!", "cut the throat!", that's the word. I defy you again. Oh hound of Crete, do you think you'll get my wife? No! Go to the hospital, and from the sweating tub of disgrace fetch out that diseased bird of Cressida's kind, Doll Tearsheet by name, and marry her. I have, and I will keep, the former Quickly as my one and only; and, in short, that's enough. Go on.

Mine host Pistol, you must come to my master, and you, / hostess. He is very sick, and would to bed. Good Bardolph, put / thy face between his sheets, and do the office of a warming-pan. / Faith, he's very ill.

Landlord Pistol, you must come to my master, and you too, hostess. He's very sick and wants to go to bed. Good Bardolph, put your red face between his sheets and do the job of a warming-pan. Honestly, he's very ill.
By my troth, he'll yield the crow a pudding one of these days. / The King has kill'd his heart. / Good husband, come home presently.
Honestly, he'll be giving the crows a meal one of these days. The King has broken his heart. Good husband, come home at once.
Come, shall I make you two friends? We must to France / together; why the devil should we keep knives to cut one / another's throats?
Come on, shall I make you two friends? We have to go to France together; why the devil should we keep knives to cut each other's throats?
Let floods o'erswell, and fiends for food howl on!
Let floods overflow and devils howl for food!
You'll pay me the eight shillings I won of you at betting?
Will you pay me the eight shillings I won from you in a bet?
Base is the slave that pays.
That now I will have: that's the humour of it.
I'll have that now; that's the humour of it.
As manhood shall compound. Push home.
As our manhood shall settle it. Thrust away.
By this sword, he that makes the first thrust, I'll kill / him; by this sword, I will.
By this sword, whoever makes the first thrust, I'll kill him; by this sword, I will.
Sword is an oath, and oaths must have their course.
"By this sword" is an oath, and oaths must take their course.
Corporal Nym, and thou wilt be friends, be friends; an / thou wilt not, why, then, be enemies with me too. Prithee, / put up.
Corporal Nym, if you'll be friends, be friends; if you won't, then be my enemy too. Please, put it away.
I shall have my eight shillings I won from you at betting?
Will I get the eight shillings I won from you in the bet?

A noble shalt thou have, and present pay; / And liquor likewise will I give to thee, / And friendship shall combine, and brotherhood. / I'll live by Nym, and Nym shall live by me. / Is not this just? For I shall sutler be / Unto the camp, and profits will accrue. / Give me thy hand.

You shall have a noble, paid on the spot, and drink as well, and friendship and brotherhood will join us. I'll live by Nym, and Nym shall live by me. Isn't that fair? For I'm going to be a supplier of food and drink to the army, and there will be profits. Give me your hand.
Well, then, that's the humour of't.
Well then, that's the humour of it.
As ever you come of women, come in quickly to Sir John. / Ah, poor heart! he is so shak'd of a burning quotidian tertian, / that it is most lamentable to behold. Sweet men, come to him.
As surely as you were born of women, come in quickly to Sir John. Oh, poor soul! He's so shaken by a burning fever that it's terribly sad to see. Sweet men, come to him.
The King hath run bad humours on the knight; that's the even / of it.
The King has given the knight a bad time; that's the long and short of it.
Nym, thou hast spoke the right. / His heart is fracted and corroborate.
Nym, you've spoken the truth. His heart is fractured and corroborated.
The King is a good king; but it must be as it may; he / passes some humours and careers.
The King is a good king, but it must be as it may; he has his moods and his wild moments.
Let us condole the knight; for, lambkins, we will live.
Let us go and grieve with the knight; for, my lambs, we will live.
'Fore God, his Grace is bold, to trust these traitors.
By God, his Grace is bold to trust these traitors.
They shall be apprehended by and by.
How smooth and even they do bear themselves! / As if allegiance in their bosoms sat / Crowned with faith and constant loyalty.
How smooth and calm they look! As if loyalty sat in their hearts, crowned with faith and constant allegiance.
The King hath note of all that they intend, / By interception which they dream not of.
The King knows everything they plan, from intercepted messages they never dream of.
Nay, but the man that was his bed-fellow, / Whom he hath dull'd and cloy'd with gracious favours, / That he should, for a foreign purse, so sell / His sovereign's life to death and treachery.
Yes, but think of the man who was his bedfellow, whom he has filled to the brim with gracious favours, that he should sell his king's life to death and treachery for a foreign purse!

Now sits the wind fair, and we will aboard. / My Lord of Cambridge, and my kind Lord of Masham, / And you, my gentle knight, give me your thoughts. / Think you not that the powers we bear with us / Will cut their passage through the force of France, / Doing the execution and the act / For which we have in head assembled them?

Now the wind is fair, and we'll go aboard. My Lord of Cambridge, my kind Lord of Masham, and you, my gentle knight, tell me your thoughts. Don't you think the forces we take with us will cut their way through the power of France and carry out the work we have raised them for?
No doubt, my liege, if each man do his best.
No doubt of it, my lord, if every man does his best.

I doubt not that, since we are well persuaded / We carry not a heart with us from hence / That grows not in a fair consent with ours, / Nor leave not one behind that doth not wish / Success and conquest to attend on us.
I don't doubt that, since we are sure we take no heart with us from here that does not agree with ours, and leave none behind that does not wish us success and conquest.
Never was monarch better fear'd and lov'd / Than is your Majesty. There's not, I think, a subject / That sits in heart-grief and uneasiness / Under the sweet shade of your government.
No monarch was ever more respected and loved than your Majesty. I don't think there is one subject who lives in grief and unease under the sweet shade of your rule.
True; those that were your father's enemies / Have steep'd their galls in honey, and do serve you / With hearts create of duty and of zeal.
True; even those who were your father's enemies have soaked their bitterness in honey and serve you with hearts made of duty and devotion.
We therefore have great cause of thankfulness, / And shall forget the office of our hand / Sooner than quittance of desert and merit / According to the weight and worthiness.
So we have great reason to be thankful, and we would sooner forget how to use our hand than forget to reward service and merit according to its weight and worth.
So service shall with steeled sinews toil, / And labour shall refresh itself with hope, / To do your Grace incessant services.
Then service will toil with muscles of steel, and labour will refresh itself with hope, to serve your Grace without rest.

We judge no less. Uncle of Exeter, / Enlarge the man committed yesterday, / That rail'd against our person. We consider / It was excess of wine that set him on, / And on his more advice we pardon him.
We expect nothing less. Uncle Exeter, release the man arrested yesterday who shouted insults against us. We think it was too much wine that set him on, and now that he is sober we pardon him.
That's mercy, but too much security. / Let him be punish'd, sovereign, lest example / Breed, by his sufferance, more of such a kind.
That's merciful, but too trusting. Let him be punished, my king, in case letting him off breeds more of the same kind.
O, let us yet be merciful.
Oh, let us still be merciful.
So may your Highness, and yet punish too.
Your Highness can be, and still punish too.
Sir, / You show great mercy if you give him life / After the taste of much correction.
Sir, you show great mercy if you let him live after giving him a good taste of punishment.

Alas, your too much love and care of me / Are heavy orisons 'gainst this poor wretch! / If little faults, proceeding on distemper, / Shall not be wink'd at, how shall we stretch our eye / When capital crimes, chew'd, swallow'd, and digested, / Appear before us? We'll yet enlarge that man, / Though Cambridge, Scroop, and Grey, in their dear care / And tender preservation of our person, / Would have him punish'd. And now to our French causes. / Who are the late commissioners?

Alas, your great love and care for me are heavy prayers against this poor wretch! If little faults that come from drunkenness are not to be overlooked, how wide shall we open our eyes when crimes worthy of death, chewed, swallowed and digested, come before us? We'll release that man all the same, though Cambridge, Scroop and Grey, in their loving care and tender protection of our person, would have him punished. And now to our French business. Who are the newly appointed commissioners?
I one, my lord. / Your Highness bade me ask for it to-day.
I am one, my lord. Your Highness told me to ask for my commission today.
So did you me, my liege.
So did you tell me, my lord.

Then, Richard Earl of Cambridge, there is yours; / There yours, Lord Scroop of Masham; and, sir knight, / Grey of Northumberland, this same is yours. / Read them, and know I know your worthiness. / My Lord of Westmoreland, and uncle Exeter, / We will aboard to-night.--Why, how now, gentlemen! / What see you in those papers that you lose / So much complexion?--Look ye, how they change! / Their cheeks are paper.--Why, what read you there, / That have so cowarded and chas'd your blood / Out of appearance?

Then, Richard Earl of Cambridge, there is yours; there's yours, Lord Scroop of Masham; and, sir knight, Grey of Northumberland, this one is yours. Read them, and know that I know what you are worth. My Lord of Westmoreland and Uncle Exeter, we'll go aboard tonight. Why, what's the matter, gentlemen? What do you see in those papers that makes you lose so much colour? Look how they change! Their cheeks are as white as paper. Why, what are you reading there that has made your blood run so cowardly out of sight?
I do confess my fault, / And do submit me to your Highness' mercy.
I confess my crime and throw myself on your Highness's mercy.

The mercy that was quick in us but late, / By your own counsel is suppress'd and kill'd. / You must not dare, for shame, to talk of mercy, / For your own reasons turn into your bosoms, / As dogs upon their masters, worrying you. / See you, my princes and my noble peers, / These English monsters! My Lord of Cambridge here, / You know how apt our love was to accord / To furnish him with all appertinents / Belonging to his honour; and this man / Hath, for a few light crowns, lightly conspir'd / And sworn unto the practices of France / To kill us here in Hampton; to the which / This knight, no less for bounty bound to us / Than Cambridge is, hath likewise sworn. But, O / What shall I say to thee, Lord Scroop? thou cruel, / Ingrateful, savage, and inhuman creature! / Thou that didst bear the key of all my counsels, / That knew'st the very bottom of my soul, / That almost mightst have coin'd me into gold, / Wouldst thou have practis'd on me for thy use,-- / May it be possible that foreign hire / Could out of thee extract one spark of evil / That might annoy my finger? 'Tis so strange, / That, though the truth of it stands off as gross / As black and white, my eye will scarcely see it. / Treason and murder ever kept together, / As two yoke-devils sworn to either's purpose, / Working so grossly in a natural cause / That admiration did not whoop at them; / But thou, 'gainst all proportion, didst bring in / Wonder to wait on treason and on murder; / And whatsoever cunning fiend it was / That wrought upon thee so preposterously / Hath got the voice in hell for excellence; / And other devils that suggest by treasons / Do botch and bungle up damnation / With patches, colours, and with forms being fetch'd / From glist'ring semblances of piety. / But he that temper'd thee bade thee stand up, / Gave thee no instance why thou shouldst do treason, / Unless to dub thee with the name of traitor. / If that same demon that hath gull'd thee thus / Should with his lion gait walk the whole world, / He might return to vasty Tartar back, / And tell the legions, "I can never win / A soul so easy as that Englishman's." / O, how hast thou with jealousy infected / The sweetness of affiance! Show men dutiful? / Why, so didst thou. Seem they grave and learned? / Why, so didst thou. Come they of noble family? / Why, so didst thou. Seem they religious? / Why, so didst thou. Or are they spare in diet, / Free from gross passion or of mirth or anger, / Constant in spirit, not swerving with the blood, / Garnish'd and deck'd in modest complement, / Not working with the eye without the ear, / And but in purged judgement trusting neither? / Such and so finely bolted didst thou seem. / And thus thy fall hath left a kind of blot / To mark the full-fraught man and best indued / With some suspicion. I will weep for thee; / For this revolt of thine, methinks, is like / Another fall of man. Their faults are open. / Arrest them to the answer of the law; / And God acquit them of their practices!

The mercy that was alive in us just now has been suppressed and killed by your own advice. For shame, you must not dare to talk of mercy, because your own arguments turn back on your hearts like dogs on their masters, tearing at you. Look, my princes and noble lords, at these English monsters! My Lord of Cambridge here, you know how ready our love was to give him everything that belonged to his rank; and this man, for a few light coins, has lightly plotted and sworn to the schemes of France to kill us here in Southampton. And this knight, no less bound to us by our generosity than Cambridge is, has sworn the same. But oh, what shall I say to you, Lord Scroop? You cruel, ungrateful, savage and inhuman creature! You who held the key to all my secrets, who knew the very bottom of my soul, who could almost have turned me into gold for your own use, could you have plotted against me for your own profit? Is it possible that foreign pay could squeeze out of you one spark of evil that might hurt my finger? It is so strange that, though the truth of it stands out as plain as black and white, my eye can hardly see it. Treason and murder have always gone together, like two devils in one yoke, each sworn to the other's purpose, working so obviously for their natural end that no one cried out in amazement at them. But you, against all reason, brought amazement in to wait on treason and murder; and whatever cunning devil worked on you so unnaturally has won the vote in hell as the best. Other devils who tempt men to treason patch together damnation with excuses, colours and shapes borrowed from glittering appearances of holiness. But the one who moulded you just told you to rise up, and gave you no reason to commit treason except to dub you with the name of traitor. If that same demon who fooled you like this were to stride the whole world with his lion's step, he might go back to vast hell and tell its legions, "I can never win a soul as easily as that Englishman's." Oh, how you have infected the sweetness of trust with suspicion! Do men seem dutiful? Why, so did you. Do they seem serious and learned? Why, so did you. Do they come of noble family? Why, so did you. Do they seem religious? Why, so did you. Or are they moderate in diet, free of coarse passions of joy or anger, steady in spirit, not carried away by impulse, dressed and adorned in modest manners, not trusting the eye without the ear, and trusting neither except after clear judgement? You seemed exactly that, so finely sifted. And so your fall has left a kind of stain that marks even the most complete and gifted man with some suspicion. I will weep for you; for this rebellion of yours seems to me like a second fall of man. Their crimes are plain. Arrest them to answer to the law; and may God forgive them for their plots!

I arrest thee of high treason, by the name of Richard Earl of / Cambridge. I arrest thee of high treason, by the name of Henry / Lord Scroop of Masham. I arrest thee of high treason, by the name / of Thomas Grey, knight, of Northumberland.

I arrest you for high treason, in the name of Richard Earl of Cambridge. I arrest you for high treason, in the name of Henry Lord Scroop of Masham. I arrest you for high treason, in the name of Thomas Grey, knight, of Northumberland.
Our purposes God justly hath discover'd, / And I repent my fault more than my death, / Which I beseech your Highness to forgive, / Although my body pay the price of it.
God has justly uncovered our plans, and I regret my crime more than my death, which I beg your Highness to forgive, even though my body pays the price for it.

For me, the gold of France did not seduce, / Although I did admit it as a motive / The sooner to effect what I intended. / But God be thanked for prevention, / Which I in sufferance heartily will rejoice, / Beseeching God and you to pardon me.

As for me, the gold of France did not tempt me, though I accepted it as a means to bring about sooner what I intended. But thank God it was prevented, which I will heartily rejoice at even while I suffer, begging God and you to pardon me.

Never did faithful subject more rejoice / At the discovery of most dangerous treason / Than I do at this hour joy o'er myself, / Prevented from a damned enterprise. / My fault, but not my body, pardon, sovereign.
No loyal subject ever rejoiced more at the discovery of a most dangerous treason than I do at this moment for myself, stopped from a damned enterprise. Pardon my crime, my king, but not my body.

God quit you in his mercy! Hear your sentence. / You have conspir'd against our royal person, / Join'd with an enemy proclaim'd, and from his coffers / Received the golden earnest of our death; / Wherein you would have sold your king to slaughter, / His princes and his peers to servitude, / His subjects to oppression and contempt, / And his whole kingdom into desolation. / Touching our person seek we no revenge; / But we our kingdom's safety must so tender, / Whose ruin you have sought, that to her laws / We do deliver you. Get you therefore hence, / Poor miserable wretches, to your death, / The taste whereof God of his mercy give / You patience to endure, and true repentance / Of all your dear offences! Bear them hence.

May God reward you with his mercy! Hear your sentence. You have plotted against our royal person, joined a declared enemy, and taken from his treasury the gold down payment for our death. In doing so you would have sold your king to slaughter, his princes and lords to slavery, his subjects to oppression and contempt, and his whole kingdom to ruin. For our own person we seek no revenge, but we must care so much for our kingdom's safety, whose ruin you have sought, that we hand you over to its laws. So go away, poor miserable wretches, to your death; and may God in his mercy give you patience to bear it and true repentance for all your grievous crimes! Take them away.

Now, lords, for France; the enterprise whereof / Shall be to you, as us, like glorious. / We doubt not of a fair and lucky war, / Since God so graciously hath brought to light / This dangerous treason lurking in our way / To hinder our beginnings. We doubt not now / But every rub is smoothed on our way. / Then forth, dear countrymen! Let us deliver / Our puissance into the hand of God, / Putting it straight in expedition. / Cheerly to sea! The signs of war advance! / No king of England, if not king of France!

Now, lords, to France; the enterprise will be as glorious for you as for us. We have no doubt of a fair and lucky war, since God has so graciously brought to light this dangerous treason lurking in our path to stop us at the start. We're sure now that every obstacle on our way has been smoothed out. So onward, dear countrymen! Let us put our strength into the hands of God and set it moving at once. Cheerfully to sea! Raise the banners of war! No king of England, if not king of France!
Prithee, honey, sweet husband, let me bring thee to Staines.
Please, honey, sweet husband, let me go with you as far as Staines.
No; for my manly heart doth yearn. / Bardolph, be blithe; Nym, rouse thy vaunting veins; / Boy, bristle thy courage up; for Falstaff he is dead, / And we must yearn therefore.
No; for my manly heart grieves. Bardolph, be cheerful; Nym, stir up your boasting spirit; boy, bristle up your courage; for Falstaff is dead, and so we must grieve.
Would I were with him, wheresome'er he is, either in / heaven or in hell!
I wish I were with him, wherever he is, whether in heaven or in hell!

Nay, sure, he's not in hell. He's in Arthur's bosom, if ever / man went to Arthur's bosom. 'A made a finer end and went / away an it had been any christom child. 'A parted even just / between twelve and one, even at the turning o' the tide: for / after I saw him fumble with the sheets, and play with flowers, / and smile upon his fingers' ends, I knew there was but one way; / for his nose was as sharp as a pen, and 'a babbled of green / fields. "How now, Sir John!" quoth I; "what, man! be o' good / cheer." So 'a cried out, "God, God, God!" three or four times. / Now I, to comfort him, bid him 'a should not think of God; I / hop'd there was no need to trouble himself with any such thoughts / yet. So 'a bade me lay more clothes on his feet. I put my hand / into the bed and felt them, and they were as cold as any stone; / then I felt to his knees, and they were as cold as any stone; / and so upward and upward, and all was as cold as any stone.

No, he's surely not in hell. He's in Arthur's bosom, if any man ever went to Arthur's bosom. He made a finer end and went away as if he were a baby just christened. He died just between twelve and one, right at the turn of the tide. For after I saw him fumble with the sheets and play with flowers and smile at his fingertips, I knew there was only one way he was going; for his nose was as sharp as a pen, and he babbled of green fields. "How are you, Sir John!" I said. "Come on, man, cheer up." Then he cried out "God, God, God!" three or four times. Now I, to comfort him, told him he shouldn't think of God; I hoped there was no need for him to trouble himself with such thoughts yet. Then he asked me to put more blankets on his feet. I put my hand into the bed and felt them, and they were as cold as any stone; then I felt up to his knees, and they were as cold as any stone; and so up and up, and everything was as cold as any stone.
They say he cried out of sack.
They say he cried out against sack.
Yes, that 'a did; and said they were devils incarnate.
Yes, he did, and said they were devils incarnate.
'A could never abide carnation; 'twas a colour he never liked.
He could never stand carnation; it was a colour he never liked.
'A said once, the devil would have him about women.
He said once the devil would get him because of women.
'A did in some sort, indeed, handle women; but then he was / rheumatic, and talk'd of the whore of Babylon.
In a way he did handle women, it's true; but then he was rheumatic, and talked about the whore of Babylon.
Do you not remember, 'a saw a flea stick upon Bardolph's nose, / and 'a said it was a black soul burning in hell-fire?
Don't you remember, he saw a flea stuck on Bardolph's nose and said it was a black soul burning in hell-fire?
Well, the fuel is gone that maintain'd that fire. That's all the / riches I got in his service.
Well, the fuel that kept that fire going is gone. That's all the riches I got in his service.
Shall we shog? The King will be gone from Southampton.
Shall we get moving? The King will have left Southampton.

Come, let's away. My love, give me thy lips. / Look to my chattels and my movables. / Let senses rule; the word is "Pitch and Pay." / Trust none; / For oaths are straws, men's faiths are wafer-cakes / And hold-fast is the only dog, my duck; / Therefore, Caveto be thy counsellor. / Go, clear thy crystals. Yoke-fellows in arms, / Let us to France; like horse-leeches, my boys, / To suck, to suck, the very blood to suck!

Come, let's go. My love, give me your lips. Look after my goods and furniture. Use your sense; the rule is "cash down". Trust no one; for oaths are straws, men's promises are thin as wafers, and Hold-fast is the only dog worth having, my duck; so let Caution be your adviser. Go, dry your eyes. Comrades in arms, let's go to France, like horse-leeches, my boys, to suck, to suck, to suck the very blood!
And that's but unwholesome food, they say.
And that's unhealthy food, they say.
Touch her soft mouth, and march.
Touch her soft mouth and march.
I cannot kiss; that is the humour of it; but, adieu.
I can't kiss, that's the humour of it; but goodbye.
Let housewifery appear. Keep close, I thee command.
Be a good housekeeper. Stay at home, I order you.

Thus comes the English with full power upon us, / And more than carefully it us concerns / To answer royally in our defences. / Therefore the Dukes of Berri and of Bretagne, / Of Brabant and of Orleans, shall make forth, / And you, Prince Dauphin, with all swift dispatch, / To line and new repair our towns of war / With men of courage and with means defendant; / For England his approaches makes as fierce / As waters to the sucking of a gulf. / It fits us then to be as provident / As fears may teach us out of late examples / Left by the fatal and neglected English / Upon our fields.

So the English are coming at us in full strength, and it matters more than ever that we answer with royal defences. So the Dukes of Berri and Brittany, of Brabant and of Orleans, shall set out, and you, Prince Dauphin, with all speed, to man and repair our fortified towns with brave soldiers and the means of defence. For England's advance is as fierce as water rushing into a whirlpool. So it suits us to be as careful as fear can teach us from recent examples left on our fields by the deadly English we underestimated.

My most redoubted father, / It is most meet we arm us 'gainst the foe; / For peace itself should not so dull a kingdom, / Though war nor no known quarrel were in question, / But that defences, musters, preparations, / Should be maintain'd, assembled, and collected, / As were a war in expectation. / Therefore, I say, 'tis meet we all go forth / To view the sick and feeble parts of France. / And let us do it with no show of fear; / No, with no more than if we heard that England / Were busied with a Whitsun morris-dance; / For, my good liege, she is so idly king'd, / Her sceptre so fantastically borne / By a vain, giddy, shallow, humorous youth, / That fear attends her not.

My most honoured father, it is right that we arm against the enemy; for even peace should not make a kingdom so dull, even if no war or quarrel were in question, that defences, musters and supplies are not kept up, gathered and collected as if a war were expected. So I say it is right that we all go out to inspect the weak and feeble parts of France. And let's do it without showing any fear; no, with no more fear than if we heard that England were busy with a Whitsun morris dance. For, my good lord, she has such an idle king, her sceptre is carried so fancifully by a vain, giddy, shallow, moody youth, that there is nothing to fear.

O peace, Prince Dauphin! / You are too much mistaken in this king. / Question your Grace the late ambassadors / With what great state he heard their embassy, / How well supplied with noble counsellors, / How modest in exception, and withal / How terrible in constant resolution, / And you shall find his vanities forespent / Were but the outside of the Roman Brutus, / Covering discretion with a coat of folly; / As gardeners do with ordure hide those roots / That shall first spring and be most delicate.

Oh, quiet, Prince Dauphin! You are badly mistaken about this king. Ask the ambassadors who have just returned, your Grace, with what great dignity he heard their message, how well supplied he was with noble advisers, how moderate in his objections, and at the same time how terrifying in his firm resolve. And you'll find his past follies were only the outward disguise of the Roman Brutus, covering wisdom with a coat of foolishness, as gardeners hide with manure the roots that will spring up first and be the most delicate.

Well, 'tis not so, my Lord High Constable; / But though we think it so, it is no matter. / In cases of defence 'tis best to weigh / The enemy more mighty than he seems, / So the proportions of defence are fill'd; / Which, of a weak and niggardly projection, / Doth, like a miser, spoil his coat with scanting / A little cloth.

Well, it isn't so, my Lord High Constable; but even if we think it is, it doesn't matter. In matters of defence it's best to judge the enemy stronger than he seems, so that our defences are fully supplied; skimping on them, like a miser, spoils the coat to save a little cloth.

Think we King Harry strong; / And, Princes, look you strongly arm to meet him. / The kindred of him hath been flesh'd upon us; / And he is bred out of that bloody strain / That haunted us in our familiar paths. / Witness our too much memorable shame / When Cressy battle fatally was struck, / And all our princes captiv'd by the hand / Of that black name, Edward, Black Prince of Wales; / Whiles that his mountain sire, on mountain standing, / Up in the air, crown'd with the golden sun, / Saw his heroical seed, and smil'd to see him, / Mangle the work of nature and deface / The patterns that by God and by French fathers / Had twenty years been made. This is a stem / Of that victorious stock; and let us fear / The native mightiness and fate of him.

Let us think King Harry strong; and, princes, make sure you arm strongly to meet him. His family has tasted our blood before, and he is bred from that bloody stock that haunted us on our own home ground. Remember our all too memorable shame when the battle of Crecy was so fatally fought, and all our princes were captured by that dreaded name, Edward, the Black Prince of Wales, while his mountain of a father, standing on a mountain high in the air, crowned with the golden sun, watched his heroic son and smiled to see him mangle the work of nature and destroy the men whom God and French fathers had spent twenty years making. This is a branch of that victorious tree; and let us fear his inborn strength and destiny.
Ambassadors from Harry King of England / Do crave admittance to your Majesty.
Ambassadors from Harry, King of England, ask to be admitted to your Majesty.
We'll give them present audience. Go, and bring them.
We'll see them at once. Go and bring them.
You see this chase is hotly follow'd, friends.
You see this hunt is being hotly pursued, friends.

Turn head and stop pursuit; for coward dogs / Most spend their mouths when what they seem to threaten / Runs far before them. Good my sovereign, / Take up the English short, and let them know / Of what a monarchy you are the head. / Self-love, my liege, is not so vile a sin / As self-neglecting.

Turn round and stop the chase; for cowardly dogs bark loudest when what they seem to threaten runs far ahead of them. My good king, cut the English short and let them know what a great monarchy you are head of. Self-love, my lord, is not so vile a sin as self-neglect.

From him; and thus he greets your Majesty: / He wills you, in the name of God Almighty, / That you divest yourself, and lay apart / The borrowed glories that by gift of heaven, / By law of nature and of nations, longs / To him and to his heirs; namely, the crown / And all wide-stretched honours that pertain / By custom and the ordinance of times / Unto the crown of France.
