That you may know / 'Tis no sinister nor no awkward claim / Pick'd from the worm-holes of long-vanish'd days, / Nor from the dust of old oblivion rak'd, / He sends you this most memorable line, / In every branch truly demonstrative; / Willing you overlook this pedigree; / And when you find him evenly deriv'd / From his most fam'd of famous ancestors, / Edward the Third, he bids you then resign / Your crown and kingdom, indirectly held / From him, the native and true challenger.

From him; and this is how he greets your Majesty. He orders you, in the name of God Almighty, to strip off and lay aside the borrowed glories that, by gift of heaven and by the law of nature and of nations, belong to him and his heirs: namely, the crown and all the wide honours that belong by custom and long tradition to the crown of France. So that you may know it is no wicked or false claim picked out of the worm-holes of long-gone days or raked out of the dust of forgotten times, he sends you this most memorable family tree, true in every branch, asking you to study it; and when you find him descended directly from his most famous of famous ancestors, Edward the Third, he orders you to give up your crown and kingdom, which you hold unlawfully from him, the born and true claimant.

Bloody constraint; for if you hide the crown / Even in your hearts, there will he rake for it. / Therefore in fierce tempest is he coming, / In thunder and in earthquake, like a Jove, / That, if requiring fail, he will compel; / And bids you, in the bowels of the Lord, / Deliver up the crown, and to take mercy / On the poor souls for whom this hungry war / Opens his vasty jaws; and on your head / Turning the widows' tears, the orphans' cries, / The dead men's blood, the pining maidens' groans, / For husbands, fathers, and betrothed lovers, / That shall be swallowed in this controversy. / This is his claim, his threat'ning, and my message; / Unless the Dauphin be in presence here, / To whom expressly I bring greeting too.

Bloody force; for if you hide the crown even in your hearts, he will dig there for it. So he is coming in a fierce storm, in thunder and earthquake, like Jove, so that if asking fails, he will force you. And he asks you, by the mercy of the Lord, to give up the crown and take pity on the poor souls for whom this hungry war is opening its huge jaws; and he turns onto your head the widows' tears, the orphans' cries, the dead men's blood and the grieving girls' groans for husbands, fathers and promised lovers who will be swallowed up in this quarrel. That is his claim, his threat and my message; except for the Dauphin, if he is here, to whom I bring a particular greeting too.
For us, we will consider of this further. / To-morrow shall you bear our full intent / Back to our brother of England.
As for us, we will think about this further. Tomorrow you shall take our full answer back to our brother of England.
For the Dauphin, / I stand here for him. What to him from England?
As for the Dauphin, I'm here for him. What message does England have for him?

Scorn and defiance. Slight regard, contempt, / And anything that may not misbecome / The mighty sender, doth he prize you at. / Thus says my king: an if your father's Highness / Do not, in grant of all demands at large, / Sweeten the bitter mock you sent his Majesty, / He'll call you to so hot an answer of it / That caves and womby vaultages of France / Shall chide your trespass and return your mock / In second accent of his ordinance.

Scorn and defiance, low regard and contempt, and anything that does not shame the mighty sender: that is what he thinks you worth. My king says this: unless your royal father sweetens the bitter joke you sent his Majesty by granting all his demands in full, he'll call you to such a hot answer for it that the caves and hollow vaults of France will rebuke your offence and throw your joke back at you in the echo of his cannon.

Say, if my father render fair return, / It is against my will; for I desire / Nothing but odds with England. To that end, / As matching to his youth and vanity, / I did present him with the Paris balls.
Tell him that if my father gives a fair answer, it is against my will; for I want nothing but a quarrel with England. That's why, to suit his youth and vanity, I sent him the Paris tennis balls.

He'll make your Paris Louvre shake for it, / Were it the mistress-court of mighty Europe; / And, be assur'd, you'll find a difference, / As we his subjects have in wonder found, / Between the promise of his greener days / And these he masters now. Now he weighs time / Even to the utmost grain. That you shall read / In your own losses, if he stay in France.

He'll make your Paris Louvre shake for it, even if it were the chief court of mighty Europe. And, believe me, you'll find a difference, as we his subjects have found with amazement, between the promise of his younger days and the man he is now. Now he weighs every moment to the last grain. You'll read that in your own losses if he stays in France.
To-morrow shall you know our mind at full.
Tomorrow you shall know our mind in full.
Dispatch us with all speed, lest that our king / Come here himself to question our delay; / For he is footed in this land already.
Send us back as fast as possible, or our king may come here himself to ask why we're delayed; for he has already set foot in this country.
You shall be soon dispatch'd with fair conditions. / A night is but small breath and little pause / To answer matters of this consequence.
You'll soon be sent back with fair terms. A night is only a short breath and a small pause to answer matters as important as this.

Thus with imagin'd wing our swift scene flies, / In motion of no less celerity / Than that of thought. Suppose that you have seen / The well-appointed king at Hampton pier / Embark his royalty, and his brave fleet / With silken streamers the young Phoebus fanning. / Play with your fancies; and in them behold / Upon the hempen tackle ship-boys climbing; / Hear the shrill whistle which doth order give / To sounds confus'd; behold the threaden sails, / Borne with the invisible and creeping wind, / Draw the huge bottoms through the furrow'd sea, / Breasting the lofty surge. O, do but think / You stand upon the rivage and behold / A city on the inconstant billows dancing; / For so appears this fleet majestical, / Holding due course to Harfleur. Follow, follow! / Grapple your minds to sternage of this navy, / And leave your England, as dead midnight still, / Guarded with grandsires, babies, and old women, / Either past or not arriv'd to pith and puissance. / For who is he, whose chin is but enrich'd / With one appearing hair, that will not follow / These cull'd and choice-drawn cavaliers to France? / Work, work your thoughts, and therein see a siege; / Behold the ordnance on their carriages, / With fatal mouths gaping on girded Harfleur. / Suppose the ambassador from the French comes back, / Tells Harry that the King doth offer him / Katharine his daughter, and with her, to dowry, / Some petty and unprofitable dukedoms. / The offer likes not; and the nimble gunner / With linstock now the devilish cannon touches,

Our quick scene flies on the wings of imagination, moving no slower than thought. Imagine you have seen the well-equipped king put his royal person aboard at the pier in Southampton, and his brave fleet fanning the young sun with silk streamers. Let your imaginations play, and in them see ship-boys climbing the rope rigging; hear the shrill whistle that gives order to the confused noise; see the woven sails, filled by the invisible, creeping wind, drawing the huge hulls through the furrowed sea, breasting the high waves. Oh, just think that you stand on the shore and see a city dancing on the restless waves; for that is how this majestic fleet looks, holding its course for Harfleur. Follow, follow! Hook your minds to the sterns of this navy and leave your England as still as dead midnight, guarded by grandfathers, babies and old women, either past or not yet come to strength and power. For who is there, with just one hair showing on his chin, who will not follow these hand-picked knights to France? Work, work your thoughts, and in them see a siege. See the cannons on their wheeled carriages, their deadly mouths gaping at encircled Harfleur. Imagine the French ambassador comes back and tells Harry that the King offers him his daughter Katharine and, as her dowry, some small, worthless dukedoms. The offer does not please, and the quick gunner now touches the devilish cannon with his match,
And down goes all before them. Still be kind, / And eke out our performance with your mind.
and everything in front of them goes down. Keep on being kind, and make up for our performance with your minds.

Once more unto the breach, dear friends, once more, / Or close the wall up with our English dead. / In peace there's nothing so becomes a man / As modest stillness and humility; / But when the blast of war blows in our ears, / Then imitate the action of the tiger; / Stiffen the sinews, summon up the blood, / Disguise fair nature with hard-favour'd rage; / Then lend the eye a terrible aspect; / Let it pry through the portage of the head / Like the brass cannon; let the brow o'erwhelm it / As fearfully as does a galled rock / O'erhang and jutty his confounded base, / Swill'd with the wild and wasteful ocean. / Now set the teeth and stretch the nostril wide, / Hold hard the breath, and bend up every spirit / To his full height. On, on, you noblest English, / Whose blood is fet from fathers of war-proof! / Fathers that, like so many Alexanders, / Have in these parts from morn till even fought, / And sheath'd their swords for lack of argument. / Dishonour not your mothers; now attest / That those whom you call'd fathers did beget you. / Be copy now to men of grosser blood, / And teach them how to war. And you, good yeomen, / Whose limbs were made in England, show us here / The mettle of your pasture; let us swear / That you are worth your breeding, which I doubt not; / For there is none of you so mean and base, / That hath not noble lustre in your eyes. / I see you stand like greyhounds in the slips, / Straining upon the start. The game's afoot! / Follow your spirit, and upon this charge / Cry, "God for Harry! England and Saint George!"

Once more into the gap in the wall, dear friends, once more, or fill the wall up with our English dead! In peace nothing suits a man so well as modest quietness and humility; but when the blast of war blows in our ears, then imitate the action of the tiger. Stiffen your muscles, call up your blood, disguise your gentle nature with grim-faced rage. Then give the eye a terrible look; let it glare through the head's gunports like a brass cannon; let the brow hang over it as fearfully as a worn-away rock overhangs and juts out over its battered base, swamped by the wild and destructive ocean. Now clench your teeth and flare your nostrils, hold your breath hard, and stretch every spirit to its full height. On, on, you noblest English, whose blood comes from fathers proved in war! Fathers who, like so many Alexanders, fought in these lands from morning till evening and put away their swords only because there was no one left to fight. Don't dishonour your mothers; prove now that the men you called fathers really were your fathers. Be an example now to men of coarser blood and teach them how to fight. And you, good yeomen, whose limbs were grown in England, show us here the quality of your feeding. Let us swear that you are worth your upbringing, which I don't doubt; for there is not one of you so low and humble that he does not have a noble shine in his eyes. I see you standing like greyhounds on the leash, straining to start. The game is on! Follow your spirit, and as you charge, cry "God for Harry! England and Saint George!"
On, on, on, on, on! To the breach, to the breach!
On, on, on, on, on! To the breach, to the breach!
Pray thee, corporal, stay. The knocks are too hot; and, for / mine own part, I have not a case of lives. The humour of it is / too hot; that is the very plain-song of it.
Please, corporal, wait. The blows are too hot, and as for me, I don't have a spare set of lives. The humour of it is too hot; that's the plain tune of it.
The plain-song is most just, for humours do abound. / "Knocks go and come; God's vassals drop and die; / And sword and shield, / In bloody field, / Doth win immortal fame."
The plain tune is very right, for there are moods aplenty. (Sings) "Blows come and go; God's servants drop and die; and sword and shield, in bloody field, win everlasting fame."
Would I were in an alehouse in London! I would give all my / fame for a pot of ale and safety.
I wish I were in an alehouse in London! I'd give all my fame for a pot of ale and safety.
And I. / "If wishes would prevail with me, / My purpose should not fail with me, / But thither would I hie."
And so would I. (Sings) "If wishes could win for me, my aim would not fail me, but there I'd hurry."
"As duly, but not as truly, / As bird doth sing on bough."
(Sings) "As eagerly, but not as truly, as a bird sings on a branch."
Up to the breach, you dogs! Avaunt, you cullions!
Up to the breach, you dogs! Get on, you scoundrels!
Be merciful, great Duke, to men of mould. / Abate thy rage, abate thy manly rage, / Abate thy rage, great Duke! / Good bawcock, bate thy rage; use lenity, sweet chuck!
Have mercy, great Duke, on men made of earth. Calm your rage, calm your manly rage, calm your rage, great Duke! Good fine fellow, calm your rage; be gentle, sweet chick!
These be good humours! Your honour wins bad humours.
These are fine moods! Your honour has foul moods.

As young as I am, I have observ'd these three swashers. I am / boy to them all three; but all they three, though they would / serve me, could not be man to me; for indeed three such antics / do not amount to a man. For Bardolph, he is white-liver'd and / red-fac'd; by the means whereof 'a faces it out, but fights not. / For Pistol, he hath a killing tongue and a quiet sword; by the / means whereof 'a breaks words, and keeps whole weapons. For / Nym, he hath heard that men of few words are the best men; and / therefore he scorns to say his prayers, lest 'a should be thought / a coward. But his few bad words are match'd with as few good / deeds; for 'a never broke any man's head but his own, and that / was against a post when he was drunk. They will steal anything, / and call it purchase. Bardolph stole a lute-case, bore it twelve / leagues, and sold it for three half-pence. Nym and Bardolph are / sworn brothers in filching, and in Calais they stole a / fire-shovel. / I knew by that piece of service the men would carry coals. They / would have me as familiar with men's pockets as their gloves or / their handkerchers; which makes much against my manhood, if I / should take from another's pocket to put into mine; for it is / plain pocketing up of wrongs. I must leave them, and seek some / better service. Their villainy goes against my weak stomach, / and therefore I must cast it up.

Young as I am, I've watched these three swaggerers. I'm servant boy to all three of them; but all three together, even if they served me, couldn't be a man to me, because three such clowns don't add up to one man. As for Bardolph, he is white-livered and red-faced, which is why he brazens it out but doesn't fight. As for Pistol, he has a killing tongue and a quiet sword, which is why he breaks his word and keeps his weapons whole. As for Nym, he has heard that men of few words are the best men, and so he refuses even to say his prayers, in case he's thought a coward. But his few bad words are matched by just as few good deeds; for he never broke any man's head but his own, and that was against a post when he was drunk. They'll steal anything and call it a bargain. Bardolph stole a lute-case, carried it thirty-six miles and sold it for three halfpence. Nym and Bardolph are sworn brothers in pilfering, and in Calais they stole a fire-shovel. I knew by that bit of work that they would put up with anything. They wanted me to be as at home in men's pockets as in their gloves or handkerchiefs, which goes badly against my manhood, if I take from another's pocket to put in mine; for it's plainly pocketing up wrongs. I must leave them and look for a better position. Their villainy turns my weak stomach, so I must throw it up.
Captain Fluellen, you must come presently to the mines. / The Duke of Gloucester would speak with you.
Captain Fluellen, you must come at once to the mines. The Duke of Gloucester wants to speak with you.

To the mines! Tell you the Duke, it is not so good to come / to the mines; for, look you, the mines is not according to the / disciplines of the war. The concavities of it is not sufficient; / for, look you, the athversary, you may discuss unto the Duke, / look you, is digt himself four yard under the countermines. By / Cheshu, I think 'a will plow up all, if there is not better / directions.

To the mines! You tell the Duke it's not so good to come to the mines; for, look you, the mines are not according to the rules of war. The tunnels are not deep enough; for, look you, the enemy, you may explain to the Duke, look you, has dug himself four yards under the countermines. By Jesus, I think he'll blow everything up if there aren't better orders.
The Duke of Gloucester, to whom the order of the siege is / given, is altogether directed by an Irishman, a very valiant / gentleman, i' faith.
The Duke of Gloucester, who has been given command of the siege, is completely guided by an Irishman, a very brave gentleman, honestly.
It is Captain Macmorris, is it not?

By Cheshu, he is an ass, as in the world. I will verify as / much in his beard. He has no more directions in the true / disciplines of the wars, look you, of the Roman disciplines, / than is a puppy-dog.
By Jesus, he's as big an ass as any in the world. I'll prove as much to his face. He knows no more about the true rules of war, look you, the Roman rules, than a puppy does.
Here 'a comes; and the Scots captain, Captain Jamy, with him.
Here he comes, and the Scottish captain, Captain Jamy, with him.

Captain Jamy is a marvellous falorous gentleman, that is / certain; and of great expedition and knowledge in the aunchient / wars, upon my particular knowledge of his directions. By Cheshu, / he will maintain his argument as well as any military man in the / world, in the disciplines of the pristine wars of the Romans.

Captain Jamy is a marvellously valiant gentleman, that's certain, and of great energy and knowledge in the ancient wars, from my own knowledge of his instructions. By Jesus, he'll hold his own in an argument as well as any soldier in the world on the rules of the ancient Roman wars.
I say good day, Captain Fluellen.
God-den to your worship, good Captain James.
Good evening to your worship, good Captain James.
How now, Captain Macmorris! have you quit the mines? / Have the pioneers given o'er?
Well, Captain Macmorris, have you left the mines? Have the diggers given up?

By Chrish, la! 'tish ill done! The work ish give over, the / trompet sound the retreat. By my hand I swear, and my / father's soul, the work ish ill done; it ish give over. I would / have blowed up the town, so Chrish save me, la! in an hour. / O, 'tish ill done, 'tish ill done; by my hand, 'tish ill done!

By Christ, ah, it's badly done! The work is given up; the trumpet sounded the retreat. I swear by my hand and my father's soul, the work is badly done; it's given up. I would have blown up the town in an hour, so Christ save me! Oh, it's badly done, it's badly done; by my hand, it's badly done!

Captain Macmorris, I beseech you now, will you voutsafe me, / look you, a few disputations with you, as partly touching or / concerning the disciplines of the war, the Roman wars, in the way / of argument, look you, and friendly communication; partly to / satisfy my opinion, and partly for the satisfaction, look you, of / my mind, as touching the direction of the military discipline; / that is the point.

Captain Macmorris, I beg you now, will you allow me, look you, a few discussions with you, partly about or concerning the rules of war, the Roman wars, by way of argument, look you, and friendly conversation; partly to satisfy my opinion, and partly for the satisfaction, look you, of my mind, about the direction of military discipline; that's the point.
It sall be vary gud, gud feith, gud captains bath: and I sall / quit you with gud leve, as I may pick occasion; that sall I, / marry.
That will be very good, by my faith, good captains both; and I'll answer you, with your permission, when I get the chance; that I will, indeed.

It is no time to discourse, so Chrish save me. The day is hot, / and the weather, and the wars, and the King, and the Dukes. It / is no time to discourse. The town is beseech'd, and the trumpet / call us to the breach, and we talk, and, be Chrish, do nothing. / 'Tis shame for us all. So God sa' me, 'tis shame to stand still; / it is shame, by my hand; and there is throats to be cut, and works / to be done; and there ish nothing done, so Chrish sa' me, la!

It's no time to talk, so Christ save me. The day is hot, and the weather, and the wars, and the King, and the Dukes. It's no time to talk. The town is besieged, and the trumpet calls us to the breach, and we talk and, by Christ, do nothing. It's a shame for all of us. So God save me, it's a shame to stand still; it's a shame, by my hand; and there are throats to cut and work to do, and nothing is being done, so Christ save me!

By the mess, ere theise eyes of mine take themselves to slomber, / I'll de gud service, or I'll lig i' the grund for it; ay, or go to / death; and I'll pay't as valorously as I may, that sall I suerly do, / that is the breff and the long. Marry, I wad full fain heard some / question 'tween you tway.

By the Mass, before these eyes of mine go to sleep, I'll do good service or lie in the ground for it; yes, or go to my death; and I'll pay it as bravely as I can, that I surely will, that's the short and long of it. Indeed, I'd very much like to hear some debate between you two.
Captain Macmorris, I think, look you, under your correction, there / is not many of your nation--
Captain Macmorris, I think, look you, if you'll allow me to say so, there are not many of your nation...
Of my nation! What ish my nation? Ish a villain, and a bastard, / and a knave, and a rascal? What ish my nation? Who talks of my / nation?
Of my nation! What is my nation? Is it a villain, and a bastard, and a knave, and a rascal? What is my nation? Who's talking about my nation?

Look you, if you take the matter otherwise than is meant, Captain / Macmorris, peradventure I shall think you do not use me with that / affability as in discretion you ought to use me, look you, being / as good a man as yourself, both in the disciplines of war, and in / the derivation of my birth, and in other particularities.

Look you, if you take the matter differently from how it's meant, Captain Macmorris, perhaps I shall think you don't treat me with the courtesy you should sensibly use towards me, look you, since I'm as good a man as you, both in the rules of war and in my family descent and in other details.
I do not know you so good a man as myself. So Chrish save me, / I will cut off your head.
I don't know that you're as good a man as me. So Christ save me, I'll cut your head off.
Gentlemen both, you will mistake each other.
Gentlemen both, you are misunderstanding each other.
The town is calling for a truce to talk.
Captain Macmorris, when there is more better opportunity to be / required, look you, I will be so bold as to tell you I know the / disciplines of war; and there is an end.
Captain Macmorris, when there's a better opportunity, look you, I'll be so bold as to tell you that I know the rules of war; and that's the end of it.

How yet resolves the governor of the town? / This is the latest parle we will admit; / Therefore to our best mercy give yourselves, / Or like to men proud of destruction / Defy us to our worst; for, as I am a soldier, / A name that in my thoughts becomes me best, / If I begin the battery once again, / I will not leave the half-achieved Harfleur / Till in her ashes she lie buried. / The gates of mercy shall be all shut up, / And the flesh'd soldier, rough and hard of heart, / In liberty of bloody hand shall range / With conscience wide as hell, mowing like grass / Your fresh fair virgins and your flow'ring infants. / What is it then to me, if impious War, / Array'd in flames like to the prince of fiends, / Do with his smirch'd complexion all fell feats / Enlink'd to waste and desolation? / What is't to me, when you yourselves are cause, / If your pure maidens fall into the hand / Of hot and forcing violation? / What rein can hold licentious wickedness / When down the hill he holds his fierce career? / We may as bootless spend our vain command / Upon the enraged soldiers in their spoil / As send precepts to the leviathan / To come ashore. Therefore, you men of Harfleur, / Take pity of your town and of your people, / Whiles yet my soldiers are in my command, / Whiles yet the cool and temperate wind of grace / O'erblows the filthy and contagious clouds / Of heady murder, spoil, and villainy. / If not, why, in a moment look to see / The blind and bloody soldier with foul hand / Defile the locks of your shrill-shrieking daughters; / Your fathers taken by the silver beards, / And their most reverend heads dash'd to the walls; / Your naked infants spitted upon pikes, / Whiles the mad mothers with their howls confus'd / Do break the clouds, as did the wives of Jewry / At Herod's bloody-hunting slaughtermen. / What say you? Will you yield, and this avoid, / Or, guilty in defence, be thus destroy'd?

What has the governor of the town decided? This is the last truce we will allow; so either surrender to our best mercy or, like men proud to be destroyed, defy us to do our worst. For, as I am a soldier, a name that I think suits me best, if I begin the bombardment again I will not leave half-conquered Harfleur until she lies buried in her ashes. The gates of mercy will all be shut, and the soldier who has tasted blood, rough and hard-hearted, will roam freely with bloody hand and a conscience as wide as hell, mowing down your fresh, fair virgins and your blossoming babies like grass. What is it to me, then, if wicked War, dressed in flames like the prince of devils, with his blackened face, does all the cruel deeds that go with destruction and ruin? What is it to me, when you yourselves are the cause, if your pure daughters fall into the hands of hot and violent rape? What rein can hold back unbridled wickedness when it charges fiercely downhill? We might as well waste our useless orders on the enraged soldiers in their looting as send commands to the whale to come ashore. So, you men of Harfleur, take pity on your town and your people while my soldiers are still under my command, while the cool, calm wind of mercy still blows away the filthy, infectious clouds of reckless murder, plunder and villainy. If not, then expect in a moment to see the blind and bloody soldier with his foul hand defile the hair of your shrieking daughters; your fathers seized by their silver beards and their most respected heads smashed against the walls; your naked babies speared on pikes, while their mad mothers break the clouds with their confused howls, as the women of Judea did at Herod's bloodthirsty butchers. What do you say? Will you surrender and avoid this, or, guilty of resisting, be destroyed like this?

Our expectation hath this day an end. / The Dauphin, whom of succours we entreated, / Returns us that his powers are yet not ready / To raise so great a siege. Therefore, great King, / We yield our town and lives to thy soft mercy. / Enter our gates; dispose of us and ours; / For we no longer are defensible.

Our hopes end today. The Dauphin, whom we begged for help, sends back word that his forces are not yet ready to lift so great a siege. So, great King, we surrender our town and our lives to your gentle mercy. Enter our gates; do what you will with us and ours; for we can no longer defend ourselves.

Open your gates. Come, uncle Exeter, / Go you and enter Harfleur; there remain, / And fortify it strongly 'gainst the French. / Use mercy to them all. For us, dear uncle, / The winter coming on, and sickness growing / Upon our soldiers, we will retire to Calais. / To-night in Harfleur will we be your guest; / To-morrow for the march are we addrest.

Open your gates. Come, Uncle Exeter, go and enter Harfleur; stay there and fortify it strongly against the French. Be merciful to them all. As for us, dear uncle, with winter coming on and sickness spreading among our soldiers, we will withdraw to Calais. Tonight we will be your guest in Harfleur; tomorrow we are ready to march.
Alice, tu as ete en Angleterre, et tu parles bien le langage.
(In French) Alice, you have been in England, and you speak the language well.
Je te prie, m'enseignez; il faut que j'apprenne a parler. / Comment appelez-vous la main en Anglois?
(In French) Please teach me; I must learn to speak it. What do you call "la main" in English?
La main? Elle est appelee de hand.
(In French) La main? It is called "de hand".
Les doigts? Ma foi, j'oublie les doigts; mais je me / souviendrai. Les doigts? Je pense qu'ils sont appeles de / fingres; oui, de fingres.
(In French) Les doigts? Goodness, I forget les doigts; but I'll remember. Les doigts? I think they're called "de fingres"; yes, "de fingres".
La main, de hand; les doigts, de fingres. Je pense que / je suis le bon ecolier; j'ai gagne deux mots d'Anglois / vitement. Comment appelez-vous les ongles?
(In French) La main, "de hand"; les doigts, "de fingres". I think I'm a good student; I've learned two words of English quickly. What do you call "les ongles"?
Les ongles? Nous les appelons de nails.
(In French) Les ongles? We call them "de nails".
De nails. Ecoutez; dites-moi, si je parle bien: de hand, / de fingres, et de nails.
(In French) "De nails". Listen; tell me if I say it well: "de hand, de fingres, and de nails".
C'est bien dit, madame; il est fort bon Anglois.
(In French) Well said, madam; that's very good English.
(In French) Tell me the English for "le bras".
D'elbow. Je m'en fais la repetition de tous les mots / que vous m'avez appris des a present.
(In French) "D'elbow". I'll repeat all the words you've taught me so far.
Il est trop difficile, madame, comme je pense.
(In French) It's too hard, madam, I think.
Excusez-moi, Alice; ecoutez: d'hand, de fingres, de / nails, d'arma, de bilbow.
(In French) Excuse me, Alice; listen: "d'hand, de fingres, de nails, d'arma, de bilbow".
O Seigneur Dieu, je m'en oublie! D'elbow. / Comment appelez-vous le col?
(In French) Oh Lord God, I forget! "D'elbow". What do you call "le col"?
De sin. Le col, de nick; le menton, de sin.
(In French) "De sin". Le col, "de nick"; le menton, "de sin".
Oui. Sauf votre honneur, en verite, vous prononcez les / mots aussi droit que les natifs d'Angleterre.
(In French) Yes. With respect, truly, you pronounce the words as correctly as the natives of England.
Je ne doute point d'apprendre, par la grace de Dieu, / et en peu de temps.
(In French) I have no doubt I'll learn, by the grace of God, and in a short time.
N'avez-vous pas deja oublie ce que je vous ai enseigne?
(In French) Haven't you already forgotten what I taught you?
Non, je reciterai a vous promptement: d'hand, de / fingres, de mails,--
(In French) No, I'll recite it to you straight away: "d'hand, de fingres, de mails",
De nails, de arm, de ilbow.
(In French) "De nails, de arm, de ilbow."
Ainsi dis-je; d'elbow, de nick, et de sin. Comment / appelez-vous le pied et la robe?
(In French) That's what I said: "d'elbow, de nick, and de sin". What do you call "le pied" and "la robe"?
De foot, madame; et de coun.

De foot et de coun! O Seigneur Dieu! ce sont mots de son / mauvais, corruptible, gros, et impudique, et non pour les / dames d'honneur d'user. Je ne voudrais prononcer ces mots / devant les seigneurs de France pour tout le monde. Foh! le / foot et le coun! Neanmoins, je reciterai une autre fois ma lecon / ensemble: d' hand, de fingres, de nails, d'arm, d'elbow, de / nick, de sin, de foot, de coun.

(In French) "De foot" and "de coun"! Oh Lord God! Those are bad-sounding words, corrupting, coarse and indecent, not for ladies of honour to use. I wouldn't say those words in front of the lords of France for all the world. Ugh! "Le foot" and "le coun"! All the same, I'll recite my whole lesson once more: "d'hand, de fingres, de nails, d'arm, d'elbow, de nick, de sin, de foot, de coun".
C'est assez pour une fois: allons-nous a diner.
(In French) That's enough for one time; let's go to dinner.
'Tis certain he hath pass'd the river Somme.
It is certain he has crossed the river Somme.
And if he be not fought withal, my lord, / Let us not live in France; let us quit all / And give our vineyards to a barbarous people.
And if we don't fight him, my lord, let's not live in France; let's give up everything and hand our vineyards to a race of barbarians.
O Dieu vivant! shall a few sprays of us, / The emptying of our fathers' luxury, / Our scions put in wild and savage stock, / Spirt up so suddenly into the clouds, / And overlook their grafters?

Living God! Shall a few offshoots of ours, the spilt seed of our ancestors' lust, our shoots grafted onto wild and savage stock, spurt up so suddenly into the clouds and look down on those who grafted them?

Normans, but bastard Normans, Norman bastards! / Mort de ma vie! if they march along / Unfought withal, but I will sell my dukedom, / To buy a slobbery and a dirty farm / In that nook-shotten isle of Albion.
Normans, but bastard Normans, Norman bastards! Death of my life! If they march on without a fight, I'll sell my dukedom to buy a muddy, dirty farm on that ragged, corner-cut island of Britain.

Dieu de batailles! where have they this mettle? / Is not their climate foggy, raw, and dull, / On whom, as in despite, the sun looks pale, / Killing their fruit with frowns? Can sodden water, / A drench for sur-rein'd jades, their barley-broth, / Decoct their cold blood to such valiant heat? / And shall our quick blood, spirited with wine, / Seem frosty? O, for honour of our land, / Let us not hang like roping icicles / Upon our houses' thatch, whiles a more frosty people / Sweat drops of gallant youth in our rich fields! / Poor we may call them in their native lords.

God of battles! Where do they get this spirit? Isn't their climate foggy, raw and dull, where the sun looks pale on them as if in spite, killing their fruit with its frowns? Can boiled water, a medicine for worn-out horses, their barley-broth beer, heat their cold blood to such brave fire? And shall our lively blood, spirited by wine, seem frosty? Oh, for the honour of our country, let's not hang like dripping icicles from the thatch of our houses, while a more frosty people sweat drops of brave youth in our rich fields! We may call our fields poor in the lords they were born with.
By faith and honour, / Our madams mock at us, and plainly say / Our mettle is bred out, and they will give / Their bodies to the lust of English youth / To new-store France with bastard warriors.

By my faith and honour, our ladies mock us and say plainly that our spirit has been bred out of us, and that they will give their bodies to the lust of English youths to restock France with bastard warriors.
They bid us to the English dancing-schools, / And teach lavoltas high, and swift corantos; / Saying our grace is only in our heels, / And that we are most lofty runaways.
They tell us to go to the English dancing schools and teach high lavoltas and quick corantos, saying our only skill is in our heels, and that we are very high-flying runaways.

Where is Montjoy the herald? Speed him hence. / Let him greet England with our sharp defiance. / Up, princes! and, with spirit of honour edged / More sharper than your swords, hie to the field! / Charles Delabreth, High Constable of France; / You Dukes of Orleans, Bourbon, and of Berri, / Alencon, Brabant, Bar, and Burgundy; / Jacques Chatillon, Rambures, Vaudemont, / Beaumont, Grandpre, Roussi, and Fauconberg, / Foix, Lestrale, Bouciqualt, and Charolois; / High dukes, great princes, barons, lords, and knights, / For your great seats now quit you of great shames. / Bar Harry England, that sweeps through our land / With pennons painted in the blood of Harfleur. / Rush on his host, as doth the melted snow / Upon the valleys, whose low vassal seat / The Alps doth spit and void his rheum upon. / Go down upon him, you have power enough, / And in a captive chariot into Rouen / Bring him our prisoner.

Where is Montjoy the herald? Send him off quickly. Let him greet England with our sharp defiance. Up, princes, and with a sense of honour sharper than your swords, hurry to the field! Charles Delabreth, High Constable of France; you Dukes of Orleans, Bourbon and Berri, Alencon, Brabant, Bar and Burgundy; Jacques Chatillon, Rambures, Vaudemont, Beaumont, Grandpre, Roussi and Fauconberg, Foix, Lestrale, Bouciqualt and Charolois; high dukes, great princes, barons, lords and knights, for the sake of your great estates, now free yourselves of great shame. Stop Harry of England, who sweeps through our land with banners painted in the blood of Harfleur. Rush on his army as melted snow rushes on the valleys, the low servant ground on which the Alps spit and pour their spittle. Fall on him, you have power enough, and bring him to Rouen as our prisoner in a captive's cart.

This becomes the great. / Sorry am I his numbers are so few, / His soldiers sick and famish'd in their march; / For I am sure, when he shall see our army, / He'll drop his heart into the sink of fear / And for achievement offer us his ransom.

This is worthy of the great. I'm sorry his numbers are so small, his soldiers sick and starving on their march; for I'm sure that when he sees our army his heart will drop into the pit of fear, and instead of victory he'll offer us his ransom.
Therefore, Lord Constable, haste on Montjoy, / And let him say to England that we send / To know what willing ransom he will give. / Prince Dauphin, you shall stay with us in Rouen.
So, Lord Constable, hurry Montjoy on, and let him tell England that we send to ask what ransom he will willingly pay. Prince Dauphin, you shall stay with us in Rouen.
Not so, I do beseech your Majesty.
Be patient, for you shall remain with us. / Now forth, Lord Constable and princes all, / And quickly bring us word of England's fall.
Be patient, for you shall stay with us. Now go, Lord Constable and all you princes, and quickly bring us news of England's fall.
How now, Captain Fluellen! come you from the bridge?
Well, Captain Fluellen! Have you come from the bridge?
I assure you, there is very excellent services committed at the / bridge.
I assure you, very excellent service has been done at the bridge.
Is the Duke of Exeter safe?
Is the Duke of Exeter safe?

The Duke of Exeter is as magnanimous as Agamemnon; and a / man that I love and honour with my soul, and my heart, and my / duty, and my live, and my living, and my uttermost power. He / is not--God be praised and blessed!--any hurt in the world; but / keeps the bridge most valiantly, with excellent discipline. There / is an aunchient lieutenant there at the pridge, I think in my / very conscience he is as valiant a man as Mark Antony; and he is / a man of no estimation in the world, but I did see him do as / gallant service.

The Duke of Exeter is as great-hearted as Agamemnon, and a man that I love and honour with my soul, and my heart, and my duty, and my life, and my living, and my utmost power. He is not, God be praised and blessed, hurt in the least, but holds the bridge most bravely, with excellent discipline. There's an ensign there at the bridge, I think in my very conscience he's as brave a man as Mark Antony; and he's a man of no reputation in the world, but I saw him do fine service.
Captain, I thee beseech to do me favours. / The Duke of Exeter doth love thee well.
Captain, I beg you to do me a favour. The Duke of Exeter thinks well of you.
Ay, I praise God; and I have merited some love at his hands.
Yes, I praise God, and I have deserved some regard from him.

Bardolph, a soldier, firm and sound of heart, / And of buxom valour, hath by cruel fate / And giddy Fortune's furious fickle wheel, / That goddess blind, / That stands upon the rolling restless stone--
Bardolph, a soldier firm and sound of heart and of lively courage, has, by cruel fate and giddy Fortune's furious fickle wheel, that blind goddess who stands on the rolling, restless stone...

By your patience, Aunchient Pistol. Fortune is painted / blind, with a muffler afore his eyes, to signify to you that / Fortune is blind; and she is painted also with a wheel, to / signify to you, which is the moral of it, that she is turning, / and inconstant, and mutability, and variation; and her foot, / look you, is fixed upon a spherical stone, which rolls, and / rolls, and rolls. In good truth, the poet makes a most excellent / description of it. Fortune is an excellent moral.

Excuse me, Ensign Pistol. Fortune is painted blind, with a scarf over his eyes, to signify to you that Fortune is blind; and she is also painted with a wheel, to signify to you, which is the moral of it, that she is turning and inconstant, and changeable and variable; and her foot, look you, is fixed on a round stone, which rolls, and rolls, and rolls. In good truth, the poet makes a most excellent description of it. Fortune is an excellent moral.

Fortune is Bardolph's foe, and frowns on him; / For he hath stolen a pax, and hanged must 'a be,-- / A damned death! / Let gallows gape for dog; let man go free, / And let not hemp his windpipe suffocate. / But Exeter hath given the doom of death / For pax of little price. / Therefore, go speak; the Duke will hear thy voice; / And let not Bardolph's vital thread be cut / With edge of penny cord and vile reproach. / Speak, captain, for his life, and I will thee requite.

Fortune is Bardolph's enemy and frowns on him; for he has stolen a pax, a holy tablet, and he must be hanged. A damned death! Let gallows gape for dogs; let men go free, and let no rope choke his windpipe. But Exeter has given the sentence of death for a pax of little value. So go and speak; the Duke will listen to you; and don't let Bardolph's thread of life be cut with a penny rope and vile disgrace. Speak for his life, captain, and I'll repay you.
Aunchient Pistol, I do partly understand your meaning.
Ensign Pistol, I partly understand what you mean.

Certainly, aunchient, it is not a thing to rejoice at; for if, / look you, he were my brother, I would desire the Duke / to use his good pleasure, and put him to execution; for / discipline ought to be used.
Certainly, ensign, it's nothing to rejoice at; for if, look you, he were my brother, I would want the Duke to do as he pleases and have him executed; for discipline must be kept.
Die and be damn'd! and figo for thy friendship!
Die and be damned! And a fig for your friendship!
Why, this is an arrant counterfeit rascal. I remember / him now; a bawd, a cutpurse.
Why, this is an out-and-out fake, a rascal. I remember him now: a pimp, a pickpocket.
I'll assure you, 'a uttered as prave words at the pridge as you / shall see in a summer's day. But it is very well; what he has / spoke to me, that is well, I warrant you, when time is serve.
I assure you, he spoke as brave words at the bridge as you'll see on a summer's day. But it is very well; what he has said to me, that is well, I promise you, when the time comes.

Why, 't is a gull, a fool, a rogue, that now and then goes to / the wars, to grace himself at his return into London under the / form of a soldier. And such fellows are perfect in the great / commanders' names; and they will learn you by rote where services / were done; at such and such a sconce, at such a breach, at such a / convoy; who came off bravely, who was shot, who disgrac'd, what / terms the enemy stood on; and this they con perfectly in the / phrase of war, which they trick up with new-tuned oaths: and what / a beard of the general's cut and a horrid suit of the camp will / do among foaming bottles and ale-wash'd wits, is wonderful to be / thought on. But you must learn to know such slanders of the age, / or else you may be marvellously mistook.

Why, he's a dupe, a fool, a rogue, who now and then goes to the wars so that he can show off on his return to London dressed as a soldier. Fellows like that know the great commanders' names perfectly, and they'll recite to you where the actions were fought: at such and such a fort, at such a breach, at such a convoy; who came off bravely, who was shot, who was disgraced, what terms the enemy held out for; and they learn this perfectly in military jargon, which they dress up with newly fashioned oaths. And what a beard trimmed like the general's and a shabby, battle-worn uniform will do among frothing bottles and ale-soaked minds is amazing to think of. But you must learn to recognise these disgraces of our time, or you can be badly fooled.

I tell you what, Captain Gower; I do perceive he is not the man / that he would gladly make show to the world he is. If I find a / hole in his coat, I will tell him my mind. [Drum heard] Hark / you, the King is coming, and I must speak with him from the pridge.

I'll tell you what, Captain Gower; I can see he isn't the man he would like to show the world he is. If I find a hole in his coat, I'll tell him what I think. (Drum heard) Listen, the King is coming, and I must give him news from the bridge.
How now, Fluellen! cam'st thou from the bridge?
Well, Fluellen! Have you come from the bridge?

Ay, so please your Majesty. The Duke of Exeter has very / gallantly maintain'd the pridge. The French is gone off, look / you; and there is gallant and most prave passages. Marry, th' / athversary was have possession of the pridge; but he is enforced / to retire, and the Duke of Exeter is master of the pridge. I can / tell your Majesty, the Duke is a prave man.

Yes, if it please your Majesty. The Duke of Exeter has held the bridge very gallantly. The French have gone off, look you, and there have been gallant and most brave actions. Indeed, the enemy had taken the bridge, but he was forced to retreat, and the Duke of Exeter is master of the bridge. I can tell your Majesty, the Duke is a brave man.
What men have you lost, Fluellen?
How many men have you lost, Fluellen?

The perdition of the athversary hath been very great, reasonable / great. Marry, for my part, I think the Duke hath lost never a / man, but one that is like to be executed for robbing a church, one / Bardolph, if your Majesty know the man. His face is all bubukles, / and whelks, and knobs, and flames o' fire; and his lips blows at / his nose, and it is like a coal of fire, sometimes plue and / sometimes red; but his nose is executed, and his fire's out.

The enemy's losses have been very great, reasonably great. Indeed, for my part, I think the Duke has not lost a single man, except one who is likely to be executed for robbing a church, one Bardolph, if your Majesty knows the man. His face is all boils and pimples and lumps and flames of fire; and his lips blow at his nose, and it's like a burning coal, sometimes blue and sometimes red; but his nose is executed, and his fire's out.

We would have all such offenders so cut off; and we give express / charge, that in our marches through the country, there be nothing / compell'd from the villages, nothing taken but paid for, none of / the French upbraided or abused in disdainful language; for when / lenity and cruelty play for a kingdom, the gentler gamester is the / soonest winner.

We would have all such offenders cut off like that; and we give strict orders that on our marches through the country nothing is to be taken from the villages by force, nothing taken without being paid for, and none of the French insulted or abused with scornful words; for when gentleness and cruelty gamble for a kingdom, the gentler player wins soonest.
You know me by my habit.
You know who I am by my uniform.
Well then I know thee. What shall I know of thee?
Well then, I know you. What shall I learn from you?

Thus says my King: Say thou to Harry of England: Though we / seem'd dead, we did but sleep; advantage is a better soldier / than rashness. Tell him we could have rebuk'd him at Harfleur, / but that we thought not good to bruise an injury till it were / full ripe. Now we speak upon our cue, and our voice is imperial. / England shall repent his folly, see his weakness, and admire our / sufferance. Bid him therefore consider of his ransom; which must / proportion the losses we have borne, the subjects we have lost, / the disgrace we have digested; which in weight to re-answer, his / pettishness would bow under. For our losses, his exchequer is too / poor; for the effusion of our blood, the muster of his kingdom / too faint a number; and for our disgrace, his own person, kneeling / at our feet, but a weak and worthless satisfaction. To this add / defiance; and tell him, for conclusion, he hath betrayed his / followers, whose condemnation is pronounc'd. So far my King and / master; so much my office.

This is what my King says: Tell Harry of England that though we seemed dead, we were only asleep; waiting for the right moment is a better soldier than rashness. Tell him we could have punished him at Harfleur, but we thought it best not to lance an injury until it was fully ripe. Now we speak on our cue, and our voice is royal. England shall regret his folly, see his weakness and wonder at our patience. So tell him to think about his ransom, which must match the losses we have suffered, the subjects we have lost, the disgrace we have swallowed; to repay that in full, his small power would collapse. For our losses his treasury is too poor; for the blood we have shed, the whole muster of his kingdom is too small a number; and for our disgrace, his own person kneeling at our feet would be only a weak and worthless compensation. Add defiance to this, and tell him finally that he has betrayed his followers, whose doom is already pronounced. So far my King and master; that is my duty done.
What is thy name? I know thy quality.
What is your name? I know your rank.

Thou dost thy office fairly. Turn thee back, / And tell thy King I do not seek him now, / But could be willing to march on to Calais / Without impeachment; for, to say the sooth, / Though 'tis no wisdom to confess so much / Unto an enemy of craft and vantage, / My people are with sickness much enfeebled, / My numbers lessen'd, and those few I have / Almost no better than so many French; / Who when they were in health, I tell thee, herald, / I thought upon one pair of English legs / Did march three Frenchmen. Yet, forgive me, God, / That I do brag thus! This your air of France / Hath blown that vice in me. I must repent. / Go therefore, tell thy master here I am; / My ransom is this frail and worthless trunk, / My army but a weak and sickly guard; / Yet, God before, tell him we will come on, / Though France himself and such another neighbour / Stand in our way. There's for thy labour, Montjoy. / Go, bid thy master well advise himself. / If we may pass, we will; if we be hind'red, / We shall your tawny ground with your red blood / Discolour; and so, Montjoy, fare you well. / The sum of all our answer is but this: / We would not seek a battle, as we are; / Nor, as we are, we say we will not shun it. / So tell your master.

You do your job well. Go back and tell your King I am not looking for him now, but would be happy to march on to Calais without being stopped; for, to tell the truth, though it isn't wise to admit so much to a cunning enemy with the advantage, my men are badly weakened by sickness, my numbers reduced, and the few I have are hardly better than so many Frenchmen; though when they were healthy, I tell you, herald, I thought one pair of English legs could march as well as three Frenchmen. Yet, God forgive me for boasting like this! This French air of yours has blown that vice into me. I must repent. So go and tell your master here I am. My ransom is this frail and worthless body, my army only a weak and sickly guard. Yet, with God leading, tell him we will come on, even if France himself and another neighbour like him stand in our way. There's something for your trouble, Montjoy. Go, tell your master to think carefully. If we may pass, we will; if we are stopped, we will stain your brown earth with your red blood. And so, Montjoy, farewell. Our whole answer comes to this: as we are, we would not seek a battle; nor, as we are, do we say we will avoid one. Tell your master that.
I shall deliver so. Thanks to your Highness.
I'll deliver it so. Thank you, your Highness.
I hope they will not come upon us now.
I hope they won't attack us now.
We are in God's hands, brother, not in theirs. / March to the bridge; it now draws toward night. / Beyond the river we'll encamp ourselves, / And on to-morrow bid them march away.
We are in God's hands, brother, not in theirs. March to the bridge; night is coming on. We'll camp beyond the river, and tomorrow we'll order them to march on.
Tut! I have the best armour of the world. / Would it were day!
Nonsense! I have the best armour in the world. I wish it were day!
You have an excellent armour; but let my horse have his due.
You have excellent armour; but give my horse his due.
It is the best horse of Europe.
It's the best horse in Europe.
My Lord of Orleans, and my Lord High Constable, you talk of / horse and armour?
My Lord of Orleans and my Lord High Constable, are you talking about horses and armour?
You are as well provided of both as any prince in the world.
You are as well supplied with both as any prince in the world.

What a long night is this! I will not change my horse with / any that treads but on four pasterns. Ca, ha! he bounds from the / earth, as if his entrails were hairs; le cheval volant, the / Pegasus, chez les narines de feu! When I bestride him, I soar, I / am a hawk. he trots the air; the earth sings when he touches it; / the basest horn of his hoof is more musical than the pipe of Hermes.

What a long night this is! I wouldn't swap my horse for any animal that walks on four hooves. Ha! He leaps off the ground as if he were stuffed with hair, like a tennis ball; the flying horse, Pegasus, with nostrils of fire! When I ride him, I soar, I'm a hawk; he trots on the air; the earth sings when he touches it; the lowest horn of his hoof is more musical than the pipe of Hermes.
He's of the colour of the nutmeg.

And of the heat of the ginger. It is a beast for Perseus. He is / pure air and fire; and the dull elements of earth and water never / appear in him, but only in patient stillness while his rider mounts / him. He is indeed a horse, and all other jades you may call beasts.

And as hot as ginger. He's a beast fit for Perseus. He's pure air and fire; the dull elements of earth and water never show in him, except in his patient stillness while his rider mounts. He is truly a horse, and you may call all other nags mere beasts.
Indeed, my lord, it is a most absolute and excellent horse.
Indeed, my lord, it's a perfect and excellent horse.
It is the prince of palfreys; his neigh is like the bidding of a / monarch, and his countenance enforces homage.
He's the prince of riding horses; his neigh is like a king's command, and his face compels respect.

Nay, the man hath no wit that cannot, from the rising of the / lark to the lodging of the lamb, vary deserved praise on my / palfrey. It is a theme as fluent as the sea; turn the sands into / eloquent tongues, and my horse is argument for them all. 'Tis / a subject for a sovereign to reason on, and for a sovereign's / sovereign to ride on; and for the world, familiar to us and / unknown, to lay apart their particular functions and wonder at / him. I once writ a sonnet in his praise and began thus: "Wonder / of nature,"--

No, the man has no wit who can't, from the lark's rising to the lamb's bedtime, vary his well-deserved praise of my horse. It's a theme as flowing as the sea; turn the grains of sand into eloquent tongues, and my horse gives them all a subject. He's a subject for a king to talk about, and for a king's king to ride; and for the whole world, known and unknown, to put aside their own business and wonder at him. I once wrote a sonnet in his praise that began, "Wonder of nature",
I have heard a sonnet begin so to one's mistress.
I've heard a sonnet to someone's mistress begin like that.
Then did they imitate that which I compos'd to my courser, / for my horse is my mistress.
Then they copied the one I wrote to my horse, for my horse is my mistress.
Me well; which is the prescript praise and perfection of a / good and particular mistress.
Carries me well; which is the proper praise and perfection of a good mistress who belongs to one man.
Nay, for methought yesterday your mistress shrewdly shook / your back.
No, because I thought yesterday your mistress shook your back badly.
O then belike she was old and gentle; and you rode, like a / kern of Ireland, your French hose off, and in your strait / strossers.
Oh, then perhaps she was old and gentle, and you rode like an Irish foot-soldier, with your French breeches off and in your tight trousers.
You have good judgment in horsemanship.
You know a lot about riding.
Be warn'd by me, then; they that ride so and ride not warily, / fall into foul bogs. I had rather have my horse to my mistress.
Then take a warning from me: those who ride like that and don't take care fall into foul bogs. I'd rather have my horse as my mistress.
I had as lief have my mistress a jade.
I'd just as soon have my mistress be a nag.
I tell thee, Constable, my mistress wears his own hair.
I tell you, Constable, my mistress wears her own hair.
I could make as true a boast as that, if I had a sow to / my mistress.
I could make as true a boast as that if I had a sow as my mistress.
"Le chien est retourne a son propre vomissement, et la / truie lavee au bourbier." Thou mak'st use of anything.
"The dog has returned to its own vomit, and the washed sow to the mud." You make use of anything.
Yet do I not use my horse for my mistress, or any such / proverb so little kin to the purpose.
Yet I don't use my horse as my mistress, or any proverb so unrelated to the point.
My Lord Constable, the armour that I saw in your tent / to-night, are those stars or suns upon it?
My Lord Constable, the armour I saw in your tent tonight, are those stars or suns on it?
Some of them will fall to-morrow, I hope.
Some of them will fall tomorrow, I hope.
And yet my sky shall not want.
And still my sky won't be short of them.
That may be, for you bear a many superfluously, and 'twere / more honour some were away.
That may be, because you carry a lot more than you need, and it would be more honourable if some were gone.
Even as your horse bears your praises; who would trot as / well, were some of your brags dismounted.
Just as your horse carries your praises; he would trot just as well if some of your boasts were dismounted.
Would I were able to load him with his desert! Will it never / be day? I will trot to-morrow a mile, and my way shall be / paved with English faces.
I wish I could load him with all he deserves! Will it never be day? Tomorrow I'll trot a mile, and my way will be paved with English faces.
I will not say so, for fear I should be fac'd out of my way. / But I would it were morning; for I would fain be about / the ears of the English.
I won't say that, in case I'm faced down and driven off my way. But I wish it were morning, because I long to be at the English.
Who will go to hazard with me for twenty prisoners?
Who'll gamble with me for twenty prisoners?
You must first go yourself to hazard, ere you have them.
You must first risk yourself before you get them.
It's midnight; I'll go and put on my armour.
He longs to eat the English.
He longs to eat the English.
I think he will eat all he kills.
I think he'll eat all he kills.
By the white hand of my lady, he's a gallant prince.
By the white hand of my lady, he's a gallant prince.
Swear by her foot that she may tread out the oath.
Swear by her foot, so that she can stamp out the oath.
He is simply the most active gentleman of France.
He is simply the most active gentleman in France.
Doing is activity; and he will still be doing.
Doing is activity, and he'll always be doing something.
He never did harm, that I heard of.
He never did any harm that I've heard of.
Nor will do none to-morrow. He will keep that good / name still.
And he won't do any tomorrow. He'll keep that good name.
I know him to be valiant.
I was told that by one that knows him better than you.
I was told that by someone who knows him better than you.
Marry, he told me so himself; and he said he car'd not / who knew it.
Why, he told me so himself; and he said he didn't care who knew it.
He needs not; it is no hidden virtue in him.
He doesn't need to; it's no hidden virtue in him.
By my faith, sir, but it is; never anybody saw it but his / lackey. 'Tis a hooded valour; and when it appears, it will / bate.
By my faith, sir, it is; nobody ever saw it except his servant. It's a hooded courage, like a hawk's; and when the hood comes off, it will flutter away.
I will cap that proverb with "There is flattery in friendship."
I'll top that proverb with "There is flattery in friendship."
And I will take up that with "Give the devil his due."
And I'll answer that with "Give the devil his due."
Well plac'd. There stands your friend for the devil; have at / the very eye of that proverb with "A pox of the devil."
Well placed: there stands your friend as the devil. I'll hit the bull's-eye of that proverb with "A plague on the devil."
You are the better at proverbs, by how much "A fool's / bolt is soon shot."
You are better at proverbs to the extent that "A fool's arrow is soon shot."
'Tis not the first time you were overshot.
It's not the first time you've been shot past.
My Lord High Constable, the English lie within fifteen / hundred paces of your tents.
My Lord High Constable, the English are camped within fifteen hundred paces of your tents.
A valiant and most expert gentleman. Would it were day! / Alas, poor Harry of England, he longs not for the dawning as / we do.
A brave and very expert gentleman. I wish it were day! Alas, poor Harry of England, he isn't longing for the dawn as we are.
What a wretched and peevish fellow is this King of England, / to mope with his fat-brain'd followers so far out of his / knowledge!
What a wretched and foolish fellow this King of England is, to wander gloomily with his thick-headed followers so far out of his depth!
If the English had any apprehension, they would run away.
If the English had any sense, they would run away.
That they lack; for if their heads had any intellectual armour, / they could never wear such heavy head-pieces.
That's what they lack; for if their heads had any intellectual armour, they could never wear such heavy helmets.
That island of England breeds very valiant creatures. Their / mastiffs are of unmatchable courage.
That island of England breeds very brave creatures. Their mastiffs are of unmatched courage.

Foolish curs, that run winking into the mouth of a Russian bear / and have their heads crush'd like rotten apples! You may as well / say, that's a valiant flea that dare eat his breakfast on the lip / of a lion.

Foolish curs that run with their eyes shut into the mouth of a Russian bear and have their heads crushed like rotten apples! You might as well say that's a brave flea that dares to eat its breakfast on a lion's lip.

Just, just; and the men do sympathize with the mastiffs in / robustious and rough coming on, leaving their wits with their wives; / and then, give them great meals of beef and iron and steel, they / will eat like wolves and fight like devils.

Exactly, exactly; and the men are like the mastiffs in charging roughly and heavily, leaving their brains with their wives; and then, give them great meals of beef and iron and steel, and they'll eat like wolves and fight like devils.
Ay, but these English are shrewdly out of beef.
Yes, but these English are badly short of beef.
Then shall we find to-morrow they have only stomachs to / eat and none to fight. Now is it time to arm. Come, shall we / about it?
Then we'll find tomorrow that they only have the stomach to eat and none to fight. Now it's time to arm. Come, shall we get on with it?
It is now two o'clock; but, let me see, by ten / We shall have each a hundred Englishmen.
It is now two o'clock; but, let me see, by ten we'll each have a hundred Englishmen.

Now entertain conjecture of a time / When creeping murmur and the poring dark / Fills the wide vessel of the universe. / From camp to camp through the foul womb of night / The hum of either army stilly sounds, / That the fix'd sentinels almost receive / The secret whispers of each other's watch; / Fire answers fire, and through their paly flames / Each battle sees the other's umber'd face; / Steed threatens steed, in high and boastful neighs / Piercing the night's dull ear; and from the tents / The armourers, accomplishing the knights, / With busy hammers closing rivets up, / Give dreadful note of preparation. / The country cocks do crow, the clocks do toll, / And the third hour of drowsy morning name. / Proud of their numbers and secure in soul, / The confident and over-lusty French / Do the low-rated English play at dice; / And chide the cripple tardy-gaited Night / Who, like a foul and ugly witch, doth limp / So tediously away. The poor condemned English, / Like sacrifices, by their watchful fires / Sit patiently and inly ruminate / The morning's danger; and their gesture sad, / Investing lank-lean cheeks and war-worn coats, / Presented them unto the gazing moon / So many horrid ghosts. O now, who will behold / The royal captain of this ruin'd band / Walking from watch to watch, from tent to tent, / Let him cry, "Praise and glory on his head!" / For forth he goes and visits all his host, / Bids them good morrow with a modest smile, / And calls them brothers, friends, and countrymen. / Upon his royal face there is no note / How dread an army hath enrounded him; / Nor doth he dedicate one jot of colour / Unto the weary and all-watched night, / But freshly looks, and over-bears attaint / With cheerful semblance and sweet majesty; / That every wretch, pining and pale before, / Beholding him, plucks comfort from his looks. / A largess universal like the sun / His liberal eye doth give to every one, / Thawing cold fear, that mean and gentle all / Behold, as may unworthiness define, / A little touch of Harry in the night. / And so our scene must to the battle fly, / Where--O for pity!--we shall much disgrace / With four or five most vile and ragged foils, / Right ill-dispos'd in brawl ridiculous, / The name of Agincourt. Yet sit and see, / Minding true things by what their mock'ries be.

Now imagine a time when creeping murmurs and the straining dark fill the wide bowl of the universe. From camp to camp, through the foul womb of night, the hum of each army sounds quietly, so that the posted sentries can almost hear the secret whispers of each other's watch. Fire answers fire, and through their pale flames each army sees the other's shadowed faces. Horse threatens horse with high, boastful neighs piercing the dull ear of night; and from the tents the armourers, fitting out the knights, closing up rivets with busy hammers, give a dreadful sound of preparation. The country cocks crow, the clocks strike and announce three o'clock in the drowsy morning. Proud of their numbers and confident in spirit, the cocky, over-eager French gamble at dice for the low-valued English, and scold the crippled, slow-footed Night, who limps away so tediously like a foul, ugly witch. The poor condemned English sit patiently like sacrifices by their watch-fires and brood inwardly on the morning's danger; and their sad bearing, along with their thin, hollow cheeks and war-worn coats, make them look to the staring moon like so many horrible ghosts. Oh, now whoever sees the royal captain of this ruined band walking from watch to watch, from tent to tent, let him cry "Praise and glory on his head!" For out he goes and visits all his army, wishes them good morning with a modest smile, and calls them brothers, friends and countrymen. On his royal face there is no sign of what a terrible army surrounds him, nor does he give up one bit of colour to the weary, sleepless night; he looks fresh and overcomes exhaustion with a cheerful look and sweet majesty, so that every wretch, pining and pale before, takes comfort from his looks when he sees him. Like the sun, his generous eye gives a gift to everyone, thawing cold fear, so that high and low alike see, as far as our poor skill can show it, a little touch of Harry in the night. And so our scene must fly to the battle, where, oh, for pity's sake, we will badly disgrace the name of Agincourt with four or five vile, ragged swords, clumsily handled in a ridiculous brawl. Still, sit and watch, imagining the real things from our imitations of them.

Gloucester, 'tis true that we are in great danger; / The greater therefore should our courage be. / Good morrow, brother Bedford. God Almighty! / There is some soul of goodness in things evil, / Would men observingly distil it out; / For our bad neighbour makes us early stirrers, / Which is both healthful and good husbandry. / Besides, they are our outward consciences, / And preachers to us all, admonishing / That we should dress us fairly for our end. / Thus may we gather honey from the weed, / And make a moral of the devil himself.

Gloucester, it's true that we are in great danger, so our courage must be all the greater. Good morning, brother Bedford. God Almighty! There is some spirit of good in bad things, if men would carefully distil it out. For our bad neighbour makes us get up early, which is both healthy and good management. Besides, they are like our consciences outside us, and preachers to us all, warning us to prepare ourselves well for our end. In this way we can gather honey from the weed and draw a moral lesson from the devil himself.
Good morrow, old Sir Thomas Erpingham: / A good soft pillow for that good white head / Were better than a churlish turf of France.
Good morning, old Sir Thomas Erpingham. A good soft pillow for that good white head would be better than a rough clod of French earth.
Not so, my liege; this lodging likes me better, / Since I may say, "Now lie I like a king."
Not so, my lord; I like this bed better, since I can say, "Now I'm lying like a king."

'Tis good for men to love their present pains / Upon example; so the spirit is eased; / And when the mind is quick'ned, out of doubt, / The organs, though defunct and dead before, / Break up their drowsy grave and newly move, / With casted slough and fresh legerity. / Lend me thy cloak, Sir Thomas. Brothers both, / Commend me to the princes in our camp; / Do my good morrow to them, and anon / Desire them all to my pavilion.

It's good for men to love their present hardships by following an example like that; it eases the spirit. And when the mind is quickened, no doubt the body's organs, though dead and sluggish before, break out of their drowsy grave and move again, like a snake that has shed its skin, with fresh nimbleness. Lend me your cloak, Sir Thomas. Brothers both, give my greetings to the princes in our camp; wish them good morning from me, and ask them all to come to my tent soon.
Shall I go with your Grace?
No, my good knight; / Go with my brothers to my lords of England. / I and my bosom must debate a while, / And then I would no other company.
No, my good knight; go with my brothers to my lords of England. My heart and I must debate a while, and then I want no other company.
The Lord in heaven bless thee, noble Harry!
The Lord in heaven bless you, noble Harry!
God-a-mercy, old heart! thou speak'st cheerfully.
Thank you, old heart! You speak cheerfully.
Discuss unto me; art thou officer? / Or art thou base, common, and popular?
Explain yourself to me: are you an officer, or are you low, common and of the people?
I am a gentleman of a company.
I am a gentleman serving in a company.
Do you trail the mighty pike?
As good a gentleman as the Emperor.
As good a gentleman as the Emperor.
Then you are a better than the King.
Then you're better than the King.

The King's a bawcock, and a heart of gold, / A lad of life, an imp of fame; / Of parents good, of fist most valiant. / I kiss his dirty shoe, and from heart-string / I love the lovely bully. What is thy name?

The King's a fine fellow and a heart of gold, a lively lad, a child of fame, of good parents, with a most brave fist. I kiss his dirty shoe, and with all my heart I love the lovely fellow. What's your name?
Le Roy! a Cornish name. Art thou of Cornish crew?
Le Roy! A Cornish name. Are you one of the Cornish lot?
Tell him I'll knock his leek about his pate / Upon Saint Davy's day.
Tell him I'll knock his leek about his head on Saint David's Day.
Do not you wear your dagger in your cap that day, lest / he knock that about yours.
Don't wear your dagger in your cap that day, or he'll knock that about yours.
I thank you. God be with you!
Thank you. God be with you!
It sorts well with your fierceness.

So! in the name of Jesu Christ, speak lower. It is the greatest / admiration in the universal world, when the true and aunchient / prerogatifes and laws of the wars is not kept. If you would take / the pains but to examine the wars of Pompey the Great, you / shall find, I warrant you, that there is no tiddle taddle nor / pibble pabble in Pompey's camp. I warrant you, you shall find the / ceremonies of the wars, and the cares of it, and the forms of it, / and the sobriety of it, and the modesty of it, to be otherwise.

Hush! In the name of Jesus Christ, speak lower. It is the greatest wonder in the whole world when the true and ancient privileges and laws of war are not kept. If you would only take the trouble to examine the wars of Pompey the Great, you will find, I promise you, that there's no tittle-tattle or babble in Pompey's camp. I promise you, you will find the ceremonies of the wars, and the cares of them, and the forms of them, and the seriousness of them, and the modesty of them, to be different.
Why, the enemy is loud; you hear him all night.
Why, the enemy is loud; you can hear him all night.
If the enemy is an ass and a fool and a prating coxcomb, is it / meet, think you, that we should also, look you, be an ass and a / fool and a prating coxcomb? In your own conscience, now?
If the enemy is an ass and a fool and a chattering idiot, is it right, do you think, that we should also, look you, be an ass and a fool and a chattering idiot? In your own conscience, now?
I pray you and beseech you that you will.
I beg and beseech you to.
Though it appear a little out of fashion, / There is much care and valour in this Welshman.
Though it seems a little old-fashioned, there is a lot of care and courage in this Welshman.
Brother John Bates, is not that the morning which breaks / yonder?
Brother John Bates, isn't that the morning breaking over there?
I think it be; but we have no great cause to desire the / approach of day.
I think so; but we haven't much reason to want the day to come.
We see yonder the beginning of the day, but I think / we shall never see the end of it. Who goes there?
We see the beginning of the day over there, but I don't think we'll ever see the end of it. Who goes there?
Which captain do you serve under?
A good old commander and a most kind gentleman. I / pray you, what thinks he of our estate?
A good old commander and a very kind gentleman. Tell me, what does he think of our situation?
Even as men wreck'd upon a sand, that look to be / wash'd off the next tide.
Just like men shipwrecked on a sandbank, who expect to be washed off by the next tide.
He hath not told his thought to the King?
He hasn't told the King what he thinks?

No; nor it is not meet he should. For though I speak it to you, / I think the King is but a man as I am. The violet smells to him / as it doth to me; the element shows to him as it doth to me; all / his senses have but human conditions. His ceremonies laid by, / in his nakedness he appears but a man; and though his affections / are higher mounted than ours, yet, when they stoop, they stoop / with the like wing. Therefore, when he sees reason of fears as we / do, his fears, out of doubt, be of the same relish as ours are; / yet, in reason, no man should possess him with any appearance of / fear, lest he, by showing it, should dishearten his army.

No, and it isn't right that he should. For, though I say it to you, I think the King is only a man, like me. The violet smells the same to him as to me; the sky looks the same to him as to me; all his senses work only as human senses do. With his ceremonies put aside, naked he appears only a man; and though his feelings fly higher than ours, when they swoop down, they swoop on the same kind of wing. So when he sees reason to be afraid, as we do, his fears no doubt taste the same as ours; yet, reasonably, no one should give him any sign of fear, in case he shows it and disheartens his army.

He may show what outward courage he will; but I believe, as / cold a night as 'tis, he could wish himself in Thames up to the / neck; and so I would he were, and I by him, at all adventures, so / we were quit here.

He can put on whatever outward courage he likes; but I believe that, cold as the night is, he would wish himself in the Thames up to his neck; and I wish he were, and I beside him, whatever the risk, so long as we were out of here.
By my troth, I will speak my conscience of the King: I think he / would not wish himself anywhere but where he is.
Honestly, I'll tell you what I really think of the King: I think he wouldn't want to be anywhere but where he is.
Then I would he were here alone; so should he be sure to be / ransomed, and a many poor men's lives saved.
Then I wish he were here alone; then he'd be sure to be ransomed, and many poor men's lives would be saved.

I dare say you love him not so ill, to wish him here alone, / howsoever you speak this to feel other men's minds. Methinks / I could not die anywhere so contented as in the King's company, / his cause being just and his quarrel honourable.

I dare say you don't dislike him so much as to wish him here alone, however you talk to test other men's minds. I think I could not die anywhere so contented as in the King's company, his cause being just and his quarrel honourable.
Ay, or more than we should seek after; for we know enough, if / we know we are the King's subjects. If his cause be wrong, our / obedience to the King wipes the crime of it out of us.
Yes, or more than we should try to find out; for we know enough if we know we are the King's subjects. If his cause is wrong, our obedience to the King wipes the crime of it off us.
