But if the cause be not good, the King himself hath a heavy / reckoning to make, when all those legs and arms and heads, chopp'd / off in a battle, shall join together at the latter day and cry all, / "We died at such a place"; some swearing, some crying for a / surgeon, some upon their wives left poor behind them, some upon the / debts they owe, some upon their children rawly left. I am afeard / there are few die well that die in a battle; for how can they / charitably dispose of anything, when blood is their argument? / Now, if these men do not die well, it will be a black matter / for the King that led them to it; who to disobey were against / all proportion of subjection.

But if the cause isn't good, the King himself has a heavy account to settle, when all those legs and arms and heads chopped off in a battle join together on Judgement Day and all cry out, "We died at such a place": some swearing, some crying for a surgeon, some for the wives they left poor behind them, some for the debts they owe, some for their children left unprovided for. I'm afraid few men die well who die in a battle; for how can they settle anything in a Christian spirit when blood is their business? Now, if these men don't die well, it will be a black matter for the King who led them to it, since to disobey him would be against all the duty of a subject.

So, if a son that is by his father sent about merchandise do / sinfully miscarry upon the sea, the imputation of his wickedness, / by your rule, should be imposed upon his father that sent him; or / if a servant, under his master's command transporting a sum of / money, be assailed by robbers and die in many irreconcil'd / iniquities, you may call the business of the master the author of / the servant's damnation. But this is not so. The King is not / bound to answer the particular endings of his soldiers, the father / of his son, nor the master of his servant; for they purpose not / their death, when they purpose their services. Besides, there is / no king, be his cause never so spotless, if it come to the / arbitrement of swords, can try it out with all unspotted soldiers. / Some peradventure have on them the guilt of premeditated and / contrived murder; some, of beguiling virgins with the broken seals / of perjury; some, making the wars their bulwark, that have before / gored the gentle bosom of Peace with pillage and robbery. Now, if / these men have defeated the law and outrun native punishment, / though they can outstrip men, they have no wings to fly from God. / War is his beadle, war is his vengeance; so that here men are / punish'd for before-breach of the King's laws in now the King's / quarrel. Where they feared the death, they have borne life away; / and where they would be safe, they perish. Then if they die / unprovided, no more is the King guilty of their damnation than he / was before guilty of those impieties for the which they are now / visited. Every subject's duty is the King's; but every subject's / soul is his own. Therefore should every soldier in the wars do as / every sick man in his bed, wash every mote out of his conscience; / and dying so, death is to him advantage; or not dying, the time was / blessedly lost wherein such preparation was gained; and in him that / escapes, it were not sin to think that, making God so free an / offer, He let him outlive that day to see His greatness and to / teach others how they should prepare.

So, if a son who is sent by his father on a trading voyage dies at sea in a state of sin, by your rule the blame for his wickedness should be laid on the father who sent him; or if a servant carrying a sum of money under his master's orders is attacked by robbers and dies with many unconfessed sins, you could call the master's business the cause of the servant's damnation. But that is not so. The King is not bound to answer for the particular ends of his soldiers, nor the father of his son, nor the master of his servant; for they don't intend their deaths when they ask for their services. Besides, there is no king, however spotless his cause, who, if it comes to settlement by the sword, can fight it out with soldiers who are all spotless. Some perhaps carry the guilt of planned and plotted murder; some of seducing virgins with broken promises; some make the wars their shelter, having earlier wounded the gentle breast of Peace with looting and robbery. Now if these men have cheated the law and escaped punishment at home, though they can outrun men, they have no wings to fly from God. War is his officer, war is his vengeance; so that here men are punished for earlier breaches of the King's laws in what is now the King's quarrel. Where they feared death, they escaped with their lives; and where they think they are safe, they die. So if they die unprepared, the King is no more guilty of their damnation than he was guilty before of the sins for which they are now punished. Every subject's duty belongs to the King, but every subject's soul is his own. So every soldier in the wars should do what every sick man in his bed does: wash every speck out of his conscience. Dying like that, death is a gain to him; or if he doesn't die, the time was blessedly spent in which such readiness was gained; and of the man who escapes, it would be no sin to think that, since he made God so free an offer, God let him outlive that day to see His greatness and to teach others how to prepare themselves.
'Tis certain, every man that dies ill, the ill upon his own head, / the King is not to answer for it.
It's certain that for every man who dies in sin the sin is on his own head; the King doesn't have to answer for it.
I do not desire he should answer for me; and yet I determine to / fight lustily for him.
I don't want him to answer for me; and yet I'm determined to fight hard for him.
I myself heard the King say he would not be ransom'd.
I heard the King say myself that he would not be ransomed.
Ay, he said so, to make us fight cheerfully; but when our / throats are cut, he may be ransom'd, and we ne'er the wiser.
Yes, he said so to make us fight cheerfully; but when our throats are cut, he may be ransomed, and we'd be none the wiser.
If I live to see it, I will never trust his word after.
If I live to see it, I'll never trust his word again.

You pay him then. That's a perilous shot out of an elder-gun, / that a poor and a private displeasure can do against a monarch! / You may as well go about to turn the sun to ice with fanning in / his face with a peacock's feather. You'll never trust his word / after! Come, 'tis a foolish saying.

So you'll pay him back! That's a dangerous shot from a pop-gun, what one poor private man's displeasure can do to a king! You might as well try to turn the sun to ice by fanning its face with a peacock's feather. You'll never trust his word again! Come on, that's a foolish thing to say.
Your reproof is something too round. I should be angry with / you, if the time were convenient.
Your criticism is a bit too blunt. I would be angry with you if this were a suitable time.
Let it be a quarrel between us if you live.
Let it be a quarrel between us, if you live.
How shall I know thee again?
How will I know you again?
Give me any gage of thine, and I will wear it in my bonnet; / then, if ever thou dar'st acknowledge it, I will make it my / quarrel.
Give me some token of yours, and I'll wear it in my cap; then, if you ever dare to acknowledge it, I'll make it my quarrel.
Here's my glove; give me another of thine.
Here's my glove; give me one of yours.
This will I also wear in my cap. If ever thou come to me / and say, after to-morrow, "This is my glove," by this hand I / will take thee a box on the ear.
I'll wear this in my cap too. If you ever come to me after tomorrow and say "This is my glove", by this hand I'll give you a box on the ear.
If ever I live to see it, I will challenge it.
If I live to see it, I'll challenge you for it.
Thou dar'st as well be hang'd.
You'd as soon dare to be hanged.
Well, I will do it, though I take thee in the King's company.
Well, I'll do it, even if I find you in the King's company.
Keep thy word; fare thee well.
Be friends, you English fools, be friends. We have / French quarrels enow, if you could tell how to reckon.
Be friends, you English fools, be friends. We have enough quarrels with the French, if you could count them.

Indeed, the French may lay twenty French crowns to one / they will beat us, for they bear them on their shoulders; but it / is no English treason to cut French crowns, and to-morrow the / King himself will be a clipper. / Upon the King! Let us our lives, our souls, / Our debts, our careful wives, / Our children, and our sins lay on the King! / We must bear all. O hard condition, / Twin-born with greatness, subject to the breath / Of every fool, whose sense no more can feel / But his own wringing! What infinite heart's-ease / Must kings neglect, that private men enjoy! / And what have kings, that privates have not too, / Save ceremony, save general ceremony? / And what art thou, thou idol Ceremony? / What kind of god art thou, that suffer'st more / Of mortal griefs than do thy worshippers? / What are thy rents? What are thy comings in? / O Ceremony, show me but thy worth! / What is thy soul of adoration? / Art thou aught else but place, degree, and form, / Creating awe and fear in other men? / Wherein thou art less happy being fear'd / Than they in fearing. / What drink'st thou oft, instead of homage sweet, / But poison'd flattery? O, be sick, great greatness, / And bid thy Ceremony give thee cure! / Think'st thou the fiery fever will go out / With titles blown from adulation? / Will it give place to flexure and low bending? / Canst thou, when thou command'st the beggar's knee, / Command the health of it? No, thou proud dream, / That play'st so subtly with a king's repose; / I am a king that find thee, and I know / 'Tis not the balm, the sceptre, and the ball, / The sword, the mace, the crown imperial, / The intertissued robe of gold and pearl, / The farced title running 'fore the King, / The throne he sits on, nor the tide of pomp / That beats upon the high shore of this world, / No, not all these, thrice-gorgeous Ceremony,-- / Not all these, laid in bed majestical, / Can sleep so soundly as the wretched slave, / Who with a body fill'd and vacant mind / Gets him to rest, cramm'd with distressful bread, / Never sees horrid night, the child of hell, / But, like a lackey, from the rise to set / Sweats in the eye of Phoebus, and all night / Sleeps in Elysium; next day after dawn, / Doth rise and help Hyperion to his horse, / And follows so the ever-running year, / With profitable labour, to his grave: / And, but for ceremony, such a wretch, / Winding up days with toil and nights with sleep, / Had the fore-hand and vantage of a king. / The slave, a member of the country's peace, / Enjoys it, but in gross brain little wots / What watch the King keeps to maintain the peace, / Whose hours the peasant best advantages.

Indeed, the French can bet twenty French crowns to one that they'll beat us, since they carry them on their shoulders. But it's no treason in England to cut French crowns, and tomorrow the King himself will be a coin-clipper. Lay it all on the King! Let us lay our lives, our souls, our debts, our worried wives, our children and our sins on the King! We must carry everything. Oh, hard condition, born twin with greatness, at the mercy of the talk of every fool who can feel nothing but his own stomach-ache! What endless peace of mind must kings go without that private men enjoy! And what do kings have that private men do not have too, except ceremony, public ceremony? And what are you, you idol Ceremony? What kind of god are you, who suffers more human griefs than your worshippers do? What are your rents? What is your income? Oh Ceremony, just show me your worth! What is the essence of the worship you get? Are you anything but rank, status and outward form, creating awe and fear in other men? In which you, being feared, are less happy than they are in fearing. What do you often drink, instead of sweet respect, except poisoned flattery? Oh, be sick, great greatness, and tell your Ceremony to cure you! Do you think the burning fever will go out at titles puffed up by flattery? Will it give way to curtseys and low bows? When you command the beggar's knee, can you command its health? No, you proud dream that plays so cunningly with a king's rest. I am a king who sees through you, and I know that it is not the holy oil, the sceptre and the orb, the sword, the mace, the imperial crown, the robe woven with gold and pearl, the stuffed-up titles announced before the King, the throne he sits on, or the tide of pomp that beats on the high shore of this world; no, not all these, thrice-gorgeous Ceremony, not all these, laid in a royal bed, can sleep as soundly as the wretched slave who, with full belly and empty mind, goes to rest, stuffed with bread earned by hard toil. He never sees horrible night, the child of hell, but like a servant sweats in the sun's eye from sunrise to sunset, and all night sleeps in paradise; next day after dawn he gets up and helps the sun god onto his horse, and so follows the ever-running year with useful labour to his grave. And except for ceremony, such a wretch, filling his days with toil and his nights with sleep, would have the upper hand and the advantage over a king. The slave, a member of the peaceful country, enjoys its peace, but in his dull brain has little idea what sleepless watch the King keeps to protect that peace, whose hours benefit the peasant most of all.
My lord, your nobles, jealous of your absence, / Seek through your camp to find you.
My lord, your nobles, worried by your absence, are searching your camp for you.
Good old knight, / Collect them all together at my tent. / I'll be before thee.
Good old knight, gather them all at my tent. I'll be there before you.

O God of battles! steel my soldiers' hearts. / Possess them not with fear. Take from them now / The sense of reckoning, if the opposed numbers / Pluck their hearts from them. Not to-day, O Lord, / O, not to-day, think not upon the fault / My father made in compassing the crown! / I Richard's body have interred new, / And on it have bestow'd more contrite tears / Than from it issued forced drops of blood. / Five hundred poor I have in yearly pay, / Who twice a day their wither'd hands hold up / Toward heaven, to pardon blood; and I have built / Two chantries, where the sad and solemn priests / Sing still for Richard's soul. More will I do; / Though all that I can do is nothing worth, / Since that my penitence comes after all, / Imploring pardon.

Oh God of battles, steel my soldiers' hearts! Don't fill them with fear. Take from them now the ability to count, in case the numbers against them pluck their hearts out. Not today, oh Lord, oh, not today, don't think about the crime my father committed in seizing the crown! I have buried Richard's body again, and shed more repentant tears on it than drops of blood were forced out of it. I pay five hundred poor people a year, who twice a day hold up their withered hands to heaven to ask pardon for that blood; and I have built two chapels where sad, solemn priests continually sing for Richard's soul. I will do more, though all I can do is worth nothing, since my repentance comes after all, begging forgiveness.
My brother Gloucester's voice? Ay; / I know thy errand, I will go with thee. / The day, my friends, and all things stay for me.
My brother Gloucester's voice? Yes, I know your errand; I'll go with you. The day, my friends and everything are waiting for me.
The sun doth gild our armour; up, my lords!
The sun is gilding our armour; up, my lords!
Montez a cheval! My horse, varlet! lackey! ha!
(In French) To horse! My horse, servant! Lackey! Ha!
Via! les eaux et la terre.
(In French) Away, over water and earth!
Rien puis? L'air et le feu.
(In French) Nothing more? Air and fire, too.
Hark, how our steeds for present service neigh!
Listen how our horses neigh to go into action now!
Mount them, and make incision in their hides, / That their hot blood may spin in English eyes, / And dout them with superfluous courage, ha!
Mount them, and cut into their hides with your spurs, so that their hot blood may spurt into English eyes and put them out with extra courage, ha!
What, will you have them weep our horses' blood? / How shall we, then, behold their natural tears?
What, will you have them weep our horses' blood? Then how shall we see their own tears?
The English are embattl'd, you French peers.
The English are drawn up for battle, you French lords.

To horse, you gallant princes! straight to horse! / Do but behold yon poor and starved band, / And your fair show shall suck away their souls, / Leaving them but the shales and husks of men. / There is not work enough for all our hands; / Scarce blood enough in all their sickly veins / To give each naked curtle-axe a stain, / That our French gallants shall to-day draw out, / And sheathe for lack of sport. Let us but blow on them, / The vapour of our valour will o'erturn them. / 'Tis positive 'gainst all exceptions, lords, / That our superfluous lackeys and our peasants, / Who in unnecessary action swarm / About our squares of battle, were enow / To purge this field of such a hilding foe, / Though we upon this mountain's basis by / Took stand for idle speculation, / But that our honours must not. What's to say? / A very little little let us do, / And all is done. Then let the trumpets sound / The tucket sonance and the note to mount; / For our approach shall so much dare the field / That England shall crouch down in fear and yield.

To horse, you gallant princes! Straight to horse! Just look at that poor, starving band over there, and your fine appearance will suck the souls out of them, leaving them only the shells and husks of men. There isn't work enough for all our hands; there's hardly blood enough in all their sickly veins to stain each bare cutlass that our French gallants will draw today and sheathe again for lack of sport. We only have to blow on them, and the breath of our courage will knock them over. It is certain beyond any objection, lords, that our spare servants and our peasants, who swarm uselessly around our battle formations, would be enough to clear this field of such a worthless enemy, while we stood by at the foot of this hill watching idly; but our honour won't allow it. What more is there to say? Let us do a very little, and it's all done. Then let the trumpets sound the call to mount; for our advance will so terrify the field that England will crouch down in fear and surrender.

Why do you stay so long, my lords of France? / Yond island carrions, desperate of their bones, / Ill-favouredly become the morning field. / Their ragged curtains poorly are let loose, / And our air shakes them passing scornfully. / Big Mars seems bankrupt in their beggar'd host, / And faintly through a rusty beaver peeps; / The horsemen sit like fixed candlesticks / With torch-staves in their hand; and their poor jades / Lob down their heads, drooping the hides and hips, / The gum down-roping from their pale-dead eyes, / And in their pale dull mouths the gimmal bit / Lies foul with chew'd grass, still, and motionless; / And their executors, the knavish crows, / Fly o'er them, all impatient for their hour. / Description cannot suit itself in words / To demonstrate the life of such a battle, / In life so lifeless as it shows itself.

Why are you waiting so long, my lords of France? Those island corpses over there, hopeless of saving their bones, make an ugly sight on the morning field. Their ragged banners hang down poorly, and our air shakes them very scornfully as it passes. Mighty Mars seems bankrupt in their beggarly army and peeps feebly through a rusty visor. The horsemen sit like fixed candlesticks with lances in their hands, and their poor nags droop their heads, their skin and hips sagging, the gum dripping from their pale, dead eyes, and in their pale, dull mouths the jointed bit lies foul with chewed grass, still and motionless; and their executioners, the rascally crows, fly over them, impatient for their hour. No words can describe the life of such an army, which looks so lifeless while still alive.
They have said their prayers, and they stay for death.
They've said their prayers, and they're waiting for death.
Shall we go send them dinners and fresh suits / And give their fasting horses provender, / And after fight with them?
Shall we send them dinners and new clothes, and give their starving horses feed, and fight them afterwards?
I stay but for my guard; on to the field! / I will the banner from a trumpet take, / And use it for my haste. Come, come, away! / The sun is high, and we outwear the day.
I'm only waiting for my standard-bearer; on to the field! I'll take a banner from a trumpeter and use it in my hurry. Come, come, away! The sun is high, and we're wasting the day.
The King himself is rode to view their battle.
The King himself has ridden out to look at their army.
Of fighting men they have full three-score thousand.
They have a full sixty thousand fighting men.
There's five to one; besides, they all are fresh.
That's five to one; and besides, they are all fresh.

God's arm strike with us! 'tis a fearful odds. / God be wi' you, princes all; I'll to my charge. / If we no more meet till we meet in heaven, / Then, joyfully, my noble Lord of Bedford, / My dear Lord Gloucester, and my good Lord Exeter, / And my kind kinsman, warriors all, adieu!

May God's arm strike on our side! These are terrible odds. God be with you, princes all; I'll go to my command. If we don't meet again until we meet in heaven, then, joyfully, my noble Lord of Bedford, my dear Lord Gloucester, my good Lord Exeter, and my kind kinsman, warriors all, goodbye!
Farewell, good Salisbury, and good luck go with thee!
Farewell, good Salisbury, and good luck go with you!
Farewell, kind lord; fight valiantly to-day! / And yet I do thee wrong to mind thee of it, / For thou art fram'd of the firm truth of valour.
Farewell, kind lord; fight bravely today! And yet I wrong you by reminding you, for you are made of the solid substance of courage.
He is as full of valour as of kindness, / Princely in both.
He is as full of courage as of kindness, princely in both.
O that we now had here / But one ten thousand of those men in England / That do no work to-day!
Oh, if only we had here now just ten thousand of those men in England who are doing no work today!

What's he that wishes so? / My cousin Westmoreland? No, my fair cousin. / If we are mark'd to die, we are enow / To do our country loss; and if to live, / The fewer men, the greater share of honour. / God's will! I pray thee, wish not one man more. / By Jove, I am not covetous for gold, / Nor care I who doth feed upon my cost; / It yearns me not if men my garments wear; / Such outward things dwell not in my desires; / But if it be a sin to covet honour, / I am the most offending soul alive. / No, faith, my coz, wish not a man from England. / God's peace! I would not lose so great an honour / As one man more, methinks, would share from me / For the best hope I have. O, do not wish one more! / Rather proclaim it, Westmoreland, through my host, / That he which hath no stomach to this fight, / Let him depart. His passport shall be made, / And crowns for convoy put into his purse. / We would not die in that man's company / That fears his fellowship to die with us. / This day is call'd the feast of Crispian. / He that outlives this day, and comes safe home, / Will stand a tip-toe when this day is named, / And rouse him at the name of Crispian. / He that shall live this day, and see old age, / Will yearly on the vigil feast his neighbours, / And say, "To-morrow is Saint Crispian." / Then will he strip his sleeve and show his scars, / And say, "These wounds I had on Crispian's day." / Old men forget; yet all shall be forgot, / But he'll remember with advantages / What feats he did that day. Then shall our names, / Familiar in his mouth as household words, / Harry the King, Bedford, and Exeter, / Warwick and Talbot, Salisbury and Gloucester, / Be in their flowing cups freshly rememb'red. / This story shall the good man teach his son; / And Crispin Crispian shall ne'er go by, / From this day to the ending of the world, / But we in it shall be remembered, / We few, we happy few, we band of brothers. / For he to-day that sheds his blood with me / Shall be my brother; be he ne'er so vile, / This day shall gentle his condition; / And gentlemen in England now a-bed / Shall think themselves accurs'd they were not here, / And hold their manhoods cheap whiles any speaks / That fought with us upon Saint Crispin's day.

Who is it who wishes that? My cousin Westmoreland? No, my fair cousin. If we are marked out to die, there are enough of us for our country to lose; and if we are to live, the fewer men, the greater share of honour. By God's will, I beg you, don't wish for one man more. By Jove, I am not greedy for gold, and I don't care who eats at my expense; it doesn't trouble me if men wear my clothes; such outward things are not what I desire. But if it is a sin to long for honour, I am the most sinful soul alive. No, honestly, cousin, don't wish for one more man from England. God's peace! I would not lose as great a share of honour as one more man would take from me, I think, for the best hope I have. Oh, don't wish for one more! Rather announce through my army, Westmoreland, that whoever has no stomach for this fight may leave. His passport will be made out, and money for his journey put in his purse. We would not die in the company of a man who is afraid to die alongside us. Today is called the feast of Crispian. He who outlives this day and comes home safe will stand on tiptoe when this day is named and rouse himself at the name of Crispian. He who lives through this day and sees old age will feast his neighbours every year on the eve of it and say, "Tomorrow is Saint Crispian's." Then he will roll up his sleeve and show his scars and say, "I got these wounds on Crispin's day." Old men forget; yet even when everything else is forgotten, he'll remember, with a few additions, what deeds he did that day. Then our names, as familiar on his lips as everyday words, Harry the King, Bedford and Exeter, Warwick and Talbot, Salisbury and Gloucester, will be freshly remembered over their overflowing cups. The good man will teach this story to his son; and Crispin Crispian shall never go by, from this day to the end of the world, without our being remembered in it: we few, we happy few, we band of brothers. For whoever sheds his blood with me today shall be my brother; however low his birth, this day will raise him to a gentleman. And gentlemen in England now in bed will think themselves cursed that they were not here, and think their manhood cheap while anyone speaks who fought with us on Saint Crispin's day.
My sovereign lord, bestow yourself with speed. / The French are bravely in their battles set, / And will with all expedience charge on us.
My sovereign lord, take your place quickly. The French are splendidly drawn up in their battalions and will charge us at any moment.
All things are ready, if our minds be so.
Everything is ready, if our minds are.
Perish the man whose mind is backward now!
Death to any man whose mind is unwilling now!
Thou dost not wish more help from England, coz?
You don't wish for more help from England, cousin?
God's will! my liege, would you and I alone, / Without more help, could fight this royal battle!
By God's will, my lord, I wish you and I alone, without more help, could fight this royal battle!
Why, now thou hast unwish'd five thousand men, / Which likes me better than to wish us one. / You know your places. God be with you all!
Why, now you have unwished five thousand men, which pleases me more than wishing us one more. You know your places. God be with you all!

Once more I come to know of thee, King Harry, / If for thy ransom thou wilt now compound, / Before thy most assured overthrow; / For certainly thou art so near the gulf, / Thou needs must be englutted. Besides, in mercy, / The Constable desires thee thou wilt mind / Thy followers of repentance; that their souls / May make a peaceful and a sweet retire / From off these fields, where, wretches, their poor bodies / Must lie and fester.

Once more I have come to learn from you, King Harry, whether you will now agree on your ransom before your certain defeat; for you are surely so close to the whirlpool that you must be swallowed up. Besides, out of mercy, the Constable asks you to remind your followers to repent, so that their souls may make a peaceful and sweet withdrawal from these fields, where their poor bodies, wretches, must lie and rot.

I pray thee, bear my former answer back: / Bid them achieve me and then sell my bones. / Good God! why should they mock poor fellows thus? / The man that once did sell the lion's skin / While the beast liv'd, was kill'd with hunting him. / A many of our bodies shall no doubt / Find native graves, upon the which, I trust, / Shall witness live in brass of this day's work; / And those that leave their valiant bones in France, / Dying like men, though buried in your dunghills, / They shall be fam'd; for there the sun shall greet them, / And draw their honours reeking up to heaven; / Leaving their earthly parts to choke your clime, / The smell whereof shall breed a plague in France. / Mark then abounding valour in our English, / That being dead, like to the bullet's grazing, / Break out into a second course of mischief, / Killing in relapse of mortality. / Let me speak proudly: tell the Constable / We are but warriors for the working-day. / Our gayness and our gilt are all besmirch'd / With rainy marching in the painful field; / There's not a piece of feather in our host-- / Good argument, I hope, we will not fly-- / And time hath worn us into slovenry; / But, by the mass, our hearts are in the trim; / And my poor soldiers tell me, yet ere night / They'll be in fresher robes, or they will pluck / The gay new coats o'er the French soldiers' heads / And turn them out of service. If they do this-- / As, if God please, they shall,--my ransom then / Will soon be levied. Herald, save thou thy labour. / Come thou no more for ransom, gentle herald. / They shall have none, I swear, but these my joints; / Which if they have as I will leave 'em them, / Shall yield them little, tell the Constable.

Please take my earlier answer back: tell them to capture me first and then sell my bones. Good God, why do they mock poor men like this? The man who once sold the lion's skin while the beast was still alive was killed hunting him. Many of our bodies, no doubt, will find graves at home, on which, I trust, brass memorials will record this day's work; and those who leave their brave bones in France, dying like men, though buried in your dunghills, will be famous; for the sun will greet them there and draw their honours steaming up to heaven, leaving their earthly parts to choke your air, and the smell will breed a plague in France. So note the overflowing courage of our English, who even when dead, like a bullet bouncing on, break out into a second round of damage, killing as they rot. Let me speak proudly: tell the Constable we are only warriors in our working clothes. Our finery and gilding are all soiled from marching in the rain over the hard field; there isn't a feather in our army (good proof, I hope, that we won't fly away), and time has worn us into scruffiness. But, by the Mass, our hearts are in good trim. And my poor soldiers tell me that before night they'll be in fresher clothes, or they'll pull the gay new coats over the French soldiers' heads and dismiss them from service. If they do this, as they will if God pleases, my ransom will soon be raised. Herald, save yourself the trouble. Don't come for ransom any more, gentle herald. They'll get none, I swear, except these limbs of mine; and if they get them in the state I'll leave them in, they'll be worth little to them. Tell the Constable that.
I shall, King Harry. And so fare thee well; / Thou never shalt hear herald any more.
I shall, King Harry. And so farewell; you will never hear a herald again.
I fear thou'lt once more come again for ransom.
I'm afraid you'll come once more for ransom.
My lord, most humbly on my knee I beg / The leading of the vaward.
My lord, most humbly on my knees I beg to lead the front line.
Take it, brave York. Now, soldiers, march away; / And how thou pleasest, God, dispose the day!
Take it, brave York. Now, soldiers, march on; and, God, decide the day as you please!
Je pense que vous etes le gentilhomme de bonne qualite.
(In French) I think you are a gentleman of high rank.
Qualitie calmie custure me! Art thou a gentleman? / What is thy name? Discuss.
"Quality"? (Repeats a nonsense refrain) Are you a gentleman? What's your name? Explain.
O, Signieur Dew should be a gentleman. / Perpend my words, O Signieur Dew, and mark: / O Signieur Dew, thou diest on point of fox, / Except, O signieur, thou do give to me / Egregious ransom.
Oh, Signieur Dew must be a gentleman. Weigh my words, oh Signieur Dew, and take note: oh Signieur Dew, you die on the point of my sword, unless, oh signieur, you give me an outrageous ransom.
O, prenez misericorde! ayez pitie de moi!
(In French) Oh, have mercy! Take pity on me!
Moy shall not serve; I will have forty moys, / Or I will fetch thy rim out at thy throat / In drops of crimson blood.
"Moy" won't do; I'll have forty moys, or I'll pull your guts out through your throat in drops of crimson blood.
Est-il impossible d'echapper la force de ton bras?
(In French) Is it impossible to escape the strength of your arm?
Brass, cur! / Thou damned and luxurious mountain goat, / Offer'st me brass?
Brass, cur! You damned, lecherous mountain goat, are you offering me brass?
Say'st thou me so? Is that a ton of moys? / Come hither, boy; ask me this slave in French / What is his name.
Is that what you say? Is that a ton of moys? Come here, boy; ask this slave in French what his name is.
(In French) Listen: what is your name?
He says his name is Master Fer.
He says his name is Master Fer.
Master Fer! I'll fer him, and firk him, and ferret him. / Discuss the same in French unto him.
Master Fer! I'll fer him, and firk him, and ferret him. Explain that to him in French.
I do not know the French for fer, and ferret, and firk.
I don't know the French for "fer", "ferret" and "firk".
Bid him prepare; for I will cut his throat.
Tell him to get ready, because I'm going to cut his throat.
(In French) What does he say, sir?
Il me commande a vous dire que vous faites vous pret; car / ce soldat ici est dispose tout a cette heure de couper votre / gorge.
(In French) He orders me to tell you to get ready, because this soldier here is inclined to cut your throat at once.
Owy, cuppele gorge, permafoy, / Peasant, unless thou give me crowns, brave crowns; / Or mangled shalt thou be by this my sword.
Yes, cut the throat, by my faith, peasant, unless you give me crowns, fine crowns; or you'll be mangled by this sword of mine.
O, je vous supplie, pour l'amour de Dieu, me pardonner! / Je suis gentilhomme de bonne maison; gardez ma vie, et / je vous donnerai deux cents ecus.
(In French) Oh, I beg you, for the love of God, pardon me! I'm a gentleman of a good family; spare my life, and I'll give you two hundred crowns.
He prays you to save his life. He is a gentleman of a good / house; and for his ransom he will give you two hundred / crowns.
He begs you to spare his life. He's a gentleman of a good family, and for his ransom he'll give you two hundred crowns.
Tell him my fury shall abate, and I / The crowns will take.
Tell him my fury shall calm down, and I'll take the crowns.
(In French) Little sir, what does he say?
Encore qu'il est contre son jurement de pardonner aucun / prisonnier; neanmoins, pour les ecus que vous l'avez promis, il / est content de vous donner la liberte, le franchisement.
(In French) That although it is against his oath to pardon any prisoner, nevertheless, for the crowns you have promised him, he is content to give you your liberty, your freedom.

Sur mes genoux je vous donne mille remercimens; et je m'estime / heureux que je suis tombe entre les mains d'un chevalier, je / pense, le plus brave, vaillant, et tres distingue seigneur / d'Angleterre.

(In French) On my knees I give you a thousand thanks; and I count myself lucky that I have fallen into the hands of a knight who is, I think, the bravest, most valiant and most distinguished lord in England.

He gives you upon his knees, a thousand thanks; and he esteems / himself happy that he hath fallen into the hands of one, as he / thinks, the most brave, valorous, and thrice-worthy signieur of / England.
He gives you a thousand thanks on his knees, and he counts himself lucky that he has fallen into the hands of the bravest, most valiant and thrice-worthy lord in England, as he thinks.
As I suck blood, I will some mercy show. / Follow me!
As I suck blood, I'll show some mercy. Follow me!

I did never know so full a voice issue from so empty a heart; but / the saying is true, "The empty vessel makes the greatest sound." / Bardolph and Nym had ten times more valour than this roaring / devil i' the old play, that every one may pare his nails with a / wooden dagger; and they are both hang'd; and so would this be, / if he durst steal anything adventurously. I must stay with the / lackeys with the luggage of our camp. The French might have a / good prey of us, if he knew of it; for there is none to guard it / but boys.

I never knew such a loud voice come out of such an empty heart; but the saying is true, "The empty pot makes the most noise." Bardolph and Nym had ten times more courage than this roaring devil from the old plays, whose nails anyone can pare with a wooden dagger; and they've both been hanged, and so would he be if he dared to steal anything boldly. I must stay with the servants and the baggage of our camp. The French could make an easy catch of us if they knew about it, because there's nobody guarding it but boys.
O Seigneur! le jour est perdu, tout est perdu!
(In French) Oh Lord! The day is lost, all is lost!
Mort de ma vie! all is confounded, all! / Reproach and everlasting shame / Sits mocking in our plumes.
Death of my life! Everything is ruined, everything! Disgrace and everlasting shame sit mocking in the plumes of our helmets.
O mechante fortune! Do not run away.
(In French) Oh, wicked fortune! Don't run away.
Why, all our ranks are broke.
Why, all our ranks are broken.
O perdurable shame! let's stab ourselves, / Be these the wretches that we play'd at dice for?
Oh, everlasting shame! Let's stab ourselves. Are these the wretches we played dice for?
Is this the king we sent to for his ransom?
Is this the king we sent to about his ransom?

Shame and eternal shame, nothing but shame! / Let's die in honour! Once more back again! / And he that will not follow Bourbon now, / Let him go hence, and with his cap in hand, / Like a base pandar, hold the chamber door / Whilst by a slave, no gentler than my dog, / His fairest daughter is contaminated.

Shame, and eternal shame, nothing but shame! Let's die with honour! Back once more! And whoever won't follow Bourbon now, let him go away, and, cap in hand like a low pimp, hold the bedroom door while his fairest daughter is defiled by a slave no nobler than my dog.
Disorder, that hath spoil'd us, friend us now! / Let us on heaps go offer up our lives.
May disorder, which has ruined us, help us now! Let's go in a mass and offer up our lives.
We are enow yet living in the field / To smother up the English in our throngs, / If any order might be thought upon.
There are still enough of us alive in the field to smother the English in our crowds, if only some order could be worked out.
The devil take order now! I'll to the throng. / Let life be short, else shame will be too long.
The devil take order now! I'm going into the thick of it. Let life be short, or shame will be too long.
Well have we done, thrice valiant countrymen. / But all's not done; yet keep the French the field.
We have done well, thrice brave countrymen. But it's not all done; the French still hold the field.
The Duke of York commends him to your Majesty.
The Duke of York sends his respects to your Majesty.
Lives he, good uncle? Thrice within this hour / I saw him down; thrice up again, and fighting. / From helmet to the spur all blood he was.
Is he alive, good uncle? Three times within this hour I saw him down, three times up again and fighting. He was all blood from helmet to spur.

In which array, brave soldier, doth he lie, / Larding the plain; and by his bloody side, / Yoke-fellow to his honour-owing wounds, / The noble Earl of Suffolk also lies. / Suffolk first died; and York, all haggled over, / Comes to him, where in gore he lay insteeped, / And takes him by the beard; kisses the gashes / That bloodily did yawn upon his face. / He cries aloud, "Tarry, my cousin Suffolk! / My soul shall thine keep company to heaven; / Tarry, sweet soul, for mine, then fly abreast, / As in this glorious and well-foughten field / We kept together in our chivalry." / Upon these words I came and cheer'd him up. / He smil'd me in the face, raught me his hand, / And, with a feeble gripe, says, "Dear my lord, / Commend my service to my sovereign." / So did he turn and over Suffolk's neck / He threw his wounded arm and kiss'd his lips; / And so espous'd to death, with blood he seal'd / A testament of noble-ending love. / The pretty and sweet manner of it forc'd / Those waters from me which I would have stopp'd; / But I had not so much of man in me, / And all my mother came into mine eyes / And gave me up to tears.

And dressed like that, brave soldier, he lies, enriching the ground with his blood; and by his bloody side, partner of his honourable wounds, lies the noble Earl of Suffolk too. Suffolk died first; and York, all hacked about, came to him where he lay steeped in blood, took him by the beard, and kissed the gashes that gaped bloodily in his face. He cried aloud, "Wait, my cousin Suffolk! My soul will keep yours company to heaven. Wait for mine, sweet soul, then fly side by side, as we kept together as knights in this glorious and hard-fought field." At these words I came and comforted him. He smiled up into my face, reached me his hand, and with a feeble grip said, "My dear lord, commend my service to my king." Then he turned and threw his wounded arm over Suffolk's neck and kissed his lips; and so, married to death, he sealed with his blood a promise of love that ended nobly. The beautiful, sweet way of it forced from me those tears I would have held back; but I didn't have enough of the man in me, and all my mother's softness came into my eyes and gave me up to tears.
I blame you not; / For, hearing this, I must perforce compound / With mistful eyes, or they will issue too.
I don't blame you; for, hearing this, I must come to terms with misty eyes, or they will weep too.
But hark! what new alarum is this same? / The French have reinforc'd their scatter'd men. / Then every soldier kill his prisoners; / Give the word through.
But listen! What is this new call to arms? The French have regrouped their scattered men. Then let every soldier kill his prisoners. Pass the order on.
Kill the poys and the luggage! 'Tis expressly against the / law of arms. 'Tis as arrant a piece of knavery, mark you now, / as can be offer't; in your conscience, now, is it not?
Kill the boys and the baggage! It's expressly against the law of arms. It's as out-and-out a piece of villainy, mark you now, as could be done; in your conscience now, isn't it?

'Tis certain there's not a boy left alive; and the cowardly / rascals that ran from the battle ha' done this slaughter. / Besides, they have burned and carried away all that was in the / King's tent; wherefore the King, most worthily, hath caus'd every / soldier to cut his prisoner's throat. O, 'tis a gallant king!

It's certain there's not a boy left alive; and the cowardly rascals who ran from the battle did this slaughter. Besides, they have burned and carried away everything that was in the King's tent; so the King, most rightly, has ordered every soldier to cut his prisoner's throat. Oh, he's a gallant king!
Ay, he was porn at Monmouth, Captain Gower. What call you / the town's name where Alexander the Pig was born?
Yes, he was born at Monmouth, Captain Gower. What do you call the name of the town where Alexander the Pig was born?
Why, I pray you, is not pig great? The pig, or the great, or the / mighty, or the huge, or the magnanimous, are all one reckonings, / save the phrase is a little variations.
Why, please, isn't "pig" great? The pig, or the great, or the mighty, or the huge, or the magnanimous all come to the same thing, except that the wording is a little different.
I think Alexander the Great was born in Macedon. His father / was called Philip of Macedon, as I take it.
I think Alexander the Great was born in Macedon. His father was called Philip of Macedon, I believe.

I think it is in Macedon where Alexander is porn. I tell you, / Captain, if you look in the maps of the 'orld, I warrant you / sall find, in the comparisons between Macedon and Monmouth, / that the situations, look you, is both alike. There is a river in / Macedon; and there is also moreover a river at Monmouth; it is / call'd Wye at Monmouth; but it is out of my prains what is the / name of the other river; but 'tis all one, 'tis alike as my fingers / is to my fingers, and there is salmons in both. If you mark / Alexander's life well, Harry of Monmouth's life is come after it / indifferent well; for there is figures in all things. Alexander, / God knows, and you know, in his rages, and his furies, and his / wraths, and his cholers, and his moods, and his displeasures, and / his indignations, and also being a little intoxicates in his prains, / did, in his ales and his angers, look you, kill his best friend, / Cleitus.

I think it is in Macedon that Alexander was born. I tell you, captain, if you look at the maps of the world, I promise you'll find, in comparing Macedon and Monmouth, that the positions, look you, are both alike. There's a river in Macedon, and there's also a river at Monmouth; it's called the Wye at Monmouth, but I can't remember the name of the other river; but it's all the same, it's as alike as my fingers are to my fingers, and there are salmon in both. If you look carefully at Alexander's life, Harry of Monmouth's life follows it fairly well; for there are parallels in all things. Alexander, God knows, and you know, in his rages and his furies and his wraths and his angers and his moods and his displeasures and his indignations, and also being a little drunk in his brain, did, in his ale and his anger, look you, kill his best friend, Cleitus.
Our King is not like him in that. He never kill'd any of / his friends.
Our King isn't like him in that. He never killed any of his friends.

It is not well done, mark you now, to take the tales out / of my mouth, ere it is made and finished. I speak but in the / figures and comparisons of it. As Alexander kill'd his friend / Cleitus, being in his ales and his cups; so also Harry Monmouth, / being in his right wits and his good judgements, turn'd away the / fat knight with the great belly doublet. He was full of jests, / and gipes, and knaveries, and mocks; I have forgot his name.

It isn't right, mark you now, to take the story out of my mouth before it's made and finished. I'm only speaking of the parallels and comparisons. As Alexander killed his friend Cleitus when he was in his ale and his cups, so also Harry of Monmouth, being in his right mind and his good judgement, turned away the fat knight with the great belly-doublet. He was full of jokes and jibes and tricks and mockery; I've forgotten his name.
That is he. I'll tell you there is good men porn at Monmouth.
That's him. I tell you, there are good men born at Monmouth.

I was not angry since I came to France / Until this instant. Take a trumpet, herald; / Ride thou unto the horsemen on yond hill. / If they will fight with us, bid them come down, / Or void the field; they do offend our sight. / If they'll do neither, we will come to them, / And make them skirr away, as swift as stones / Enforced from the old Assyrian slings. / Besides, we'll cut the throats of those we have, / And not a man of them that we shall take / Shall taste our mercy. Go and tell them so.

I have not been angry since I came to France until this moment. Take a trumpeter, herald, and ride to the horsemen on that hill over there. If they want to fight us, tell them to come down, or leave the field; they offend our sight. If they'll do neither, we'll come to them and make them scurry away as fast as stones shot from the old Assyrian slings. Besides, we'll cut the throats of the prisoners we have, and not a man of those we take shall taste our mercy. Go and tell them so.
Here comes the herald of the French, my liege.
Here comes the French herald, my lord.
His eyes are humbler than they us'd to be.
His eyes are humbler than they used to be.
How now! what means this, herald? Know'st thou not / That I have fin'd these bones of mine for ransom? / Com'st thou again for ransom?
Well! What does this mean, herald? Don't you know that I have fixed these bones of mine as my ransom? Have you come for ransom again?

No, great King; / I come to thee for charitable license, / That we may wander o'er this bloody field / To book our dead, and then to bury them; / To sort our nobles from our common men. / For many of our princes--woe the while!-- / Lie drown'd and soak'd in mercenary blood; / So do our vulgar drench their peasant limbs / In blood of princes; and their wounded steeds / Fret fetlock deep in gore, and with wild rage / Yerk out their armed heels at their dead masters, / Killing them twice. O, give us leave, great King, / To view the field in safety, and dispose / Of their dead bodies!

No, great King; I come to ask your charitable permission to walk over this bloody field to record our dead and then bury them, and to sort our nobles from our common men. For many of our princes, alas, lie drowned and soaked in the blood of hired soldiers; and our common men soak their peasant limbs in the blood of princes; and their wounded horses struggle fetlock-deep in gore and in wild rage kick out with their armoured heels at their dead masters, killing them twice. Oh, give us permission, great King, to look over the field in safety and dispose of their dead bodies!
I tell thee truly, herald, / I know not if the day be ours or no; / For yet a many of your horsemen peer / And gallop o'er the field.
I tell you truly, herald, I don't know if the day is ours or not; for many of your horsemen still appear and gallop over the field.
Praised be God, and not our strength, for it! / What is this castle call'd that stands hard by?
Praise God for it, and not our strength! What is that castle called that stands close by?
Then call we this the field of Agincourt, / Fought on the day of Crispin Crispianus.
Then we'll call this the field of Agincourt, fought on the day of Crispin Crispianus.
Your grandfather of famous memory, an't please your / Majesty, and your great-uncle Edward the Plack Prince of / Wales, as I have read in the chronicles, fought a most prave / pattle here in France.
Your grandfather of famous memory, if it please your Majesty, and your great-uncle Edward the Black Prince of Wales, as I have read in the chronicles, fought a most brave battle here in France.

Your Majesty says very true. If your Majesties is rememb'red of / it, the Welshmen did good service in garden where leeks did grow, / wearing leeks in their Monmouth caps; which, your Majesty know, / to this hour is an honourable badge of the service; and I do / believe your Majesty takes no scorn to wear the leek upon Saint / Tavy's day.

Your Majesty says very true. If your Majesty remembers it, the Welshmen did good service in a garden where leeks grew, wearing leeks in their Monmouth caps; which, as your Majesty knows, is to this day an honourable badge of the service; and I believe your Majesty is not too proud to wear the leek on Saint David's Day.
I wear it for a memorable honour; / For I am Welsh, you know, good countryman.
I wear it as an honour to remember; for I am Welsh, you know, good countryman.
All the water in Wye cannot wash your Majesty's Welsh plood out / of your pody, I can tell you that. Got pless it and preserve it, / as long as it pleases His grace, and His majesty too!
All the water in the Wye can't wash your Majesty's Welsh blood out of your body, I can tell you that. God bless it and preserve it, as long as it pleases His grace, and His majesty too!

By Jeshu, I am your Majesty's countryman, I care not who know it. / I will confess it to all the 'orld. I need not be asham'd of your / Majesty, praised be God, so long as your Majesty is an honest man.
By Jesus, I am your Majesty's countryman, I don't care who knows it. I'll confess it to the whole world. I needn't be ashamed of your Majesty, praise God, as long as your Majesty is an honest man.
Our heralds go with him; / Bring me just notice of the numbers dead / On both our parts. Call yonder fellow hither.
Let our heralds go with him; bring me an exact count of the numbers dead on both sides. Call that fellow over here.
Soldier, you must come to the King.
Soldier, you must come to the King.
Soldier, why wear'st thou that glove in thy cap?
Soldier, why are you wearing that glove in your cap?
An't please your Majesty, 'tis the gage of one that I / should fight withal, if he be alive.
If it please your Majesty, it's the token of a man I'm supposed to fight, if he's alive.

An't please your Majesty, a rascal that swagger'd with me / last night; who, if alive and ever dare to challenge this / glove, I have sworn to take him a box o' the ear; or if I can / see my glove in his cap, which he swore, as he was a soldier, / he would wear if alive, I will strike it out soundly.

If it please your Majesty, a rascal who swaggered at me last night; if he's alive and ever dares to claim this glove, I've sworn to give him a box on the ear; or if I see my glove in his cap, which he swore as a soldier he would wear if he lived, I'll knock it out soundly.
What think you, Captain Fluellen? Is it fit this soldier keep / his oath?
What do you think, Captain Fluellen? Is it right for this soldier to keep his oath?
He is a craven and a villain else, an't please your Majesty, in / my conscience.
He's a coward and a villain otherwise, if it please your Majesty, in my conscience.
It may be his enemy is a gentleman of great sort, quite from / the answer of his degree.
It may be that his enemy is a gentleman of high rank, quite above answering a challenge from a man of his class.

Though he be as good a gentleman as the devil is, as Lucifier / and Belzebub himself, it is necessary, look your Grace, that he / keep his vow and his oath. If he be perjur'd, see you now, his / reputation is as arrant a villain and a Jacksauce, as ever his / black shoe trod upon God's ground and His earth, in my / conscience, la!

Even if he's as good a gentleman as the devil is, as Lucifer and Beelzebub himself, it is necessary, look your Grace, that he keeps his vow and his oath. If he breaks it, see you now, his reputation is that of as out-and-out a villain and a saucy knave as ever trod on God's ground and His earth with his black shoe, in my conscience, la!
Then keep thy vow, sirrah, when thou meet'st the fellow.
Then keep your vow, fellow, when you meet the man.
So I will, my liege, as I live.
I will, my lord, as I live.
Gower is a good captain, and is good knowledge and / literatured in the wars.
Gower is a good captain, and is well informed and well read in the wars.
Call him hither to me, soldier.
Call him here to me, soldier.

Here, Fluellen; wear thou this favour for me and stick it in thy / cap. When Alencon and myself were down together, I pluck'd / this glove from his helm. If any man challenge this, he is a / friend to Alencon, and an enemy to our person. If thou encounter / any such, apprehend him, an thou dost me love.

Here, Fluellen, wear this token for me and stick it in your cap. When Alencon and I were down on the ground together, I pulled this glove off his helmet. If any man challenges it, he is a friend of Alencon's and an enemy of ours. If you meet anyone like that, arrest him, if you love me.

Your Grace doo's me as great honours as can be desir'd in the / hearts of his subjects. I would fain see the man, that has but / two legs, that shall find himself aggrief'd at this glove; that / is all. But I would fain see it once, an please God of His grace / that I might see.

Your Grace does me as great an honour as any of his subjects could wish for in their hearts. I would like to see the man with only two legs who will take offence at this glove, that's all. But I would like to see it once, if it please God of His grace that I might.
He is my dear friend, an please you.
He's my dear friend, if you please.
Pray thee, go seek him, and bring him to my tent.
Please go and find him and bring him to my tent.

My Lord of Warwick, and my brother Gloucester, / Follow Fluellen closely at the heels. / The glove which I have given him for a favour / May haply purchase him a box o' the ear. / It is the soldier's; I by bargain should / Wear it myself. Follow, good cousin Warwick. / If that the soldier strike him, as I judge / By his blunt bearing he will keep his word, / Some sudden mischief may arise of it; / For I do know Fluellen valiant / And, touch'd with choler, hot as gunpowder, / And quickly will return an injury. / Follow, and see there be no harm between them. / Go you with me, uncle of Exeter.

My Lord of Warwick and my brother Gloucester, follow close on Fluellen's heels. The glove I've given him as a token may well earn him a box on the ear. It's the soldier's; by our bargain I should be wearing it myself. Follow, good cousin Warwick. If the soldier strikes him, and I judge from his blunt manner that he'll keep his word, some sudden trouble may come of it; for I know Fluellen is brave, and when stirred to anger is as hot as gunpowder and quick to return an injury. Follow, and make sure no harm comes between them. Come with me, Uncle Exeter.
I warrant it is to knight you, Captain.
I bet it's to knight you, Captain.
God's will and his pleasure, captain, I beseech you now, / come apace to the King. There is more good toward you / peradventure than is in your knowledge to dream of.
By God's will and pleasure, captain, I beg you now, come quickly to the King. There may be more good coming to you than you could dream of.
Sir, do you know this glove?
Know the glove! I know the glove is a glove.
Know the glove! I know the glove is a glove.
I know this; and thus I challenge it.
I know this one; and this is how I challenge it.
'Sblood! an arrant traitor as any is in the universal / world, or in France, or in England!
By God's blood! As out-and-out a traitor as any in the whole world, or in France, or in England!
Do you think I'll be forsworn?
Do you think I'll break my oath?
Stand away, Captain Gower. I will give treason his / payment into plows, I warrant you.
Stand back, Captain Gower. I'll pay treason what it's owed in blows, I promise you.
That's a lie in thy throat. I charge you in his Majesty's / name, apprehend him; he's a friend of the Duke Alencon's.
That's a lie in your throat. I order you in his Majesty's name, arrest him; he's a friend of the Duke of Alencon's.
How now, how now! what's the matter?
What's this, what's this! What's the matter?
My lord of Warwick, here is--praised be God for it!--a most / contagious treason come to light, look you, as you shall / desire in a summer's day. Here is his Majesty.
My Lord of Warwick, here is, praise God for it, a most infectious treason brought to light, look you, as fine as you could wish on a summer's day. Here is his Majesty.
My liege, here is a villain and a traitor, that, look your Grace, / has struck the glove which your Majesty is take out of the / helmet of Alencon.
My lord, here is a villain and a traitor who, look your Grace, has struck the glove which your Majesty took out of Alencon's helmet.

My liege, this was my glove; here is the fellow of it; and he / that I gave it to in change promis'd to wear it in his cap. I / promis'd to strike him, if he did. I met this man with my / glove in his cap, and I have been as good as my word.

My lord, this was my glove; here's its partner; and the man I gave it to in exchange promised to wear it in his cap. I promised to hit him if he did. I met this man with my glove in his cap, and I've been as good as my word.

Your Majesty hear now, saving your Majesty's manhood, / what an arrant, rascally, beggarly, lousy knave it is. I hope / your Majesty is pear me testimony and witness, and will / avouchment, that this is the glove of Alencon that your / Majesty is give me; in your conscience, now?

Now your Majesty hears, saving your Majesty's manhood, what an out-and-out, rascally, beggarly, lousy rogue this is. I hope your Majesty will bear me witness and testify that this is the glove of Alencon that your Majesty gave me; in your conscience, now?
Give me thy glove, soldier. Look, here is the fellow of it. / 'Twas I, indeed, thou promisedst to strike; / And thou hast given me most bitter terms.
Give me your glove, soldier. Look, here is its partner. It was me, in fact, you promised to hit, and you gave me some very harsh words.
An it please your Majesty, let his neck answer for it, if / there is any martial law in the world.
If it please your Majesty, let his neck answer for it, if there's any military law in the world.
How canst thou make me satisfaction?
How can you make amends to me?
All offences, my lord, come from the heart. Never came / any from mine that might offend your Majesty.
All offences, my lord, come from the heart. None ever came from mine that could offend your Majesty.
It was ourself thou didst abuse.

Your Majesty came not like yourself. You appear'd to me / but as a common man; witness the night, your garments, your / lowliness; and what your Highness suffer'd under that shape, I / beseech you take it for your own fault and not mine; for had you / been as I took you for, I made no offence; therefore, I beseech / your Highness, pardon me.

Your Majesty didn't come as yourself. You seemed to me only a common man; witness the darkness, your clothes, your humble manner; and whatever your Highness suffered in that shape, I beg you to take it as your own fault and not mine; for if you had been what I took you for, I did nothing wrong. So I beg your Highness, pardon me.

Here, uncle Exeter, fill this glove with crowns, / And give it to this fellow. Keep it, fellow; / And wear it for an honour in thy cap / Till I do challenge it. Give him his crowns; / And, captain, you must needs be friends with him.

Here, Uncle Exeter, fill this glove with crowns and give it to this fellow. Keep it, fellow, and wear it as an honour in your cap until I challenge it. Give him his crowns. And, captain, you must make friends with him.

By this day and this light, the fellow has mettle enough in his / belly. Hold, there is twelve pence for you; and I pray you to / serve God, and keep you out of prawls, and prabbles, and / quarrels, and dissensions, and, I warrant you, it is the better / for you.

By this day and this light, the fellow has courage enough in his belly. Here, there's twelve pence for you; and I beg you to serve God and keep out of brawls and squabbles and quarrels and arguments, and, I promise you, you'll be the better for it.
I will none of your money.

It is with a good will; I can tell you, it will serve you to mend / your shoes. Come, wherefore should you be so pashful? Your / shoes is not so good. 'Tis a good silling, I warrant you, or I / will change it.
It's given with goodwill; I can tell you, it will do to mend your shoes. Come, why should you be so shy? Your shoes aren't that good. It's a good shilling, I promise you, or I'll change it.
Now, herald, are the dead numb'red?
Now, herald, are the dead counted?
Here is the number of the slaught'red French.
Here is the number of the slaughtered French.
What prisoners of good sort are taken, uncle?
What prisoners of high rank have been taken, uncle?
Charles Duke of Orleans, nephew to the King; / John Duke of Bourbon, and Lord Bouciqualt: / Of other lords and barons, knights and squires, / Full fifteen hundred, besides common men.
Charles Duke of Orleans, nephew to the King; John Duke of Bourbon, and Lord Bouciqualt; of other lords and barons, knights and squires, a full fifteen hundred, as well as common men.

This note doth tell me of ten thousand French / That in the field lie slain; of princes, in this number, / And nobles bearing banners, there lie dead / One hundred twenty-six; added to these, / Of knights, esquires, and gallant gentlemen, / Eight thousand and four hundred; of the which, / Five hundred were but yesterday dubb'd knights; / So that, in these ten thousand they have lost, / There are but sixteen hundred mercenaries; / The rest are princes, barons, lords, knights, squires, / And gentlemen of blood and quality. / The names of those their nobles that lie dead: / Charles Delabreth, High Constable of France; / Jacques of Chatillon, Admiral of France; / The master of the cross-bows, Lord Rambures; / Great Master of France, the brave Sir Guichard Dauphin, / John Duke of Alencon, Anthony Duke of Brabant, / The brother to the Duke of Burgundy, / And Edward Duke of Bar; of lusty earls, / Grandpre and Roussi, Fauconberg and Foix, / Beaumont and Marle, Vaudemont and Lestrale. / Here was a royal fellowship of death! / Where is the number of our English dead?

This list tells me of ten thousand French who lie dead on the field. Of princes and nobles with their own banners, a hundred and twenty-six lie dead among them; and besides these, eight thousand four hundred knights, squires and gallant gentlemen, five hundred of whom were knighted only yesterday. So among these ten thousand they have lost, there are only sixteen hundred hired soldiers; the rest are princes, barons, lords, knights, squires and gentlemen of good birth and rank. These are the names of their nobles who lie dead: Charles Delabreth, High Constable of France; Jacques of Chatillon, Admiral of France; the master of the crossbowmen, Lord Rambures; the Great Master of France, brave Sir Guichard Dauphin; John Duke of Alencon; Anthony Duke of Brabant, the brother of the Duke of Burgundy; and Edward Duke of Bar; and of vigorous earls, Grandpre and Roussi, Fauconberg and Foix, Beaumont and Marle, Vaudemont and Lestrale. This was a royal company of death! Where is the count of our English dead?

Edward the Duke of York, the Earl of Suffolk, / Sir Richard Ketly, Davy Gam, esquire; / None else of name; and of all other men / But five and twenty.--O God, thy arm was here; / And not to us, but to thy arm alone, / Ascribe we all! When, without stratagem, / But in plain shock and even play of battle, / Was ever known so great and little loss / On one part and on the other? Take it, God, / For it is none but thine!

Edward the Duke of York, the Earl of Suffolk, Sir Richard Ketly, Davy Gam, squire; no one else of rank; and of all other men only twenty-five. Oh God, your arm was here; and we give all the credit not to ourselves but to your arm alone! When, without any trick, but in a straight clash and fair fight of battle, was so great a loss on one side and so little on the other ever known? Take it, God, for it is yours alone!
Come, go we in procession to the village; / And be it death proclaimed through our host / To boast of this or take that praise from God / Which is His only.
Come, let's go to the village in procession; and let it be announced through our army that it is death to boast of this or take from God the praise that belongs to Him alone.
Is it not lawful, an please your Majesty, to tell how / many is kill'd?
Isn't it lawful, if it please your Majesty, to say how many were killed?
Yes, Captain; but with this acknowledgment, / That God fought for us.
Yes, captain, but with this acknowledgement: that God fought for us.
Yes, my conscience, He did us great good.
Yes, on my conscience, He did us great good.
Do we all holy rites. / Let there be sung Non nobis and Te Deum, / The dead with charity enclos'd in clay, / And then to Calais; and to England then, / Where ne'er from France arriv'd more happy men.
Let us perform all the holy rites. Let "Non nobis" and "Te Deum" be sung, the dead buried lovingly in the earth, and then to Calais, and then to England, where happier men never arrived from France.

Vouchsafe to those that have not read the story, / That I may prompt them; and of such as have, / I humbly pray them to admit the excuse / Of time, of numbers, and due course of things, / Which cannot in their huge and proper life / Be here presented. Now we bear the King / Toward Calais; grant him there; there seen, / Heave him away upon your winged thoughts / Athwart the sea. Behold, the English beach / Pales in the flood with men, with wives and boys, / Whose shouts and claps out-voice the deep-mouth'd sea, / Which like a mighty whiffler 'fore the King / Seems to prepare his way. So let him land, / And solemnly see him set on to London. / So swift a pace hath thought that even now / You may imagine him upon Blackheath, / Where that his lords desire him to have borne / His bruised helmet and his bended sword / Before him through the city. He forbids it, / Being free from vainness and self-glorious pride; / Giving full trophy, signal, and ostent / Quite from himself to God. But now behold, / In the quick forge and working-house of thought, / How London doth pour out her citizens! / The mayor and all his brethren in best sort, / Like to the senators of the antique Rome, / With the plebeians swarming at their heels, / Go forth and fetch their conquering Caesar in; / As, by a lower but loving likelihood, / Were now the general of our gracious empress, / As in good time he may, from Ireland coming, / Bringing rebellion broached on his sword, / How many would the peaceful city quit, / To welcome him! Much more, and much more cause, / Did they this Harry. Now in London place him; / As yet the lamentation of the French / Invites the King of England's stay at home,-- / The Emperor's coming in behalf of France, / To order peace between them;--and omit / All the occurrences, whatever chanc'd, / Till Harry's back-return again to France. / There must we bring him; and myself have play'd / The interim, by rememb'ring you 'tis past. / Then brook abridgment, and your eyes advance / After your thoughts, straight back again to France.

Allow those who have not read the story to let me prompt them; and as for those who have, I humbly ask them to excuse our handling of time, of numbers and of the proper course of events, which cannot be shown here in their huge, true life. Now we carry the King towards Calais. Imagine him there; and having seen him there, lift him on your winged thoughts across the sea. Look, the English beach is fenced in at the water's edge with men, wives and boys, whose shouts and clapping drown out the deep-voiced sea, which, like a mighty usher clearing a path before the King, seems to prepare his way. So let him land, and see him set off solemnly for London. Thought moves so fast that even now you can imagine him on Blackheath, where his lords want him to have his dented helmet and his bent sword carried before him through the city. He forbids it, being free of vanity and self-glorifying pride, and gives all the trophies, signs and display away from himself to God. But now see, in the quick forge and workshop of thought, how London pours out her citizens! The mayor and all his fellow aldermen in their best clothes, like the senators of ancient Rome, with the common people swarming at their heels, go out and bring in their conquering Caesar. Just as, to take a lesser but loving comparison, if the general of our gracious queen were now coming from Ireland, as in good time he may, with rebellion skewered on his sword, how many would leave the peaceful city to welcome him! Much more, and with much more reason, did they welcome this Harry. Now place him in London, while the grief of the French still keeps the King of England at home, with the Emperor coming on France's behalf to arrange peace between them; and skip over everything that happened, whatever it was, until Harry's return to France. That's where we must bring him; and I have acted out the interval by reminding you that it has passed. So put up with the shortening, and let your eyes follow your thoughts straight back again to France.
Nay, that's right; but why wear you your leek to-day? / Saint Davy's day is past.
Yes, that's right; but why are you wearing your leek today? Saint David's Day is over.

There is occasions and causes why and wherefore in all / things. I will tell you asse my friend, Captain Gower. The / rascally, scald, beggarly, lousy, pragging knave, Pistol, which / you and yourself and all the world know to be no petter than a / fellow, look you now, of no merits, he is come to me and prings / me pread and salt yesterday, look you, and bid me eat my leek. / It was in a place where I could not breed no contention with him; / but I will be so bold as to wear it in my cap till I see him once / again, and then I will tell him a little piece of my desires.

There are occasions and causes, why and wherefore, in all things. I'll tell you, as my friend, Captain Gower. The rascally, scabby, beggarly, lousy, bragging rogue Pistol, whom you and yourself and all the world know to be no better than a fellow, look you now, of no merit, came to me yesterday and brought me bread and salt, look you, and told me to eat my leek. It was in a place where I couldn't start a quarrel with him; but I'll be so bold as to wear it in my cap until I see him again, and then I'll tell him a little of what I'd like.
Why, here he comes, swelling like a turkey-cock.
Why, here he comes, puffed up like a turkey-cock.
'Tis no matter for his swellings nor his turkey-cocks. God / pless you, Aunchient Pistol! you scurvy, lousy knave, God / pless you!
His puffings and his turkey-cocks don't matter. God bless you, Ensign Pistol! You scurvy, lousy rogue, God bless you!
Ha! art thou bedlam? Dost thou thirst, base Troyan, / To have me fold up Parca's fatal web? / Hence! I am qualmish at the smell of leek.
Ha! Are you mad? Do you thirst, you low Trojan, to have me fold up the fatal web of the Fates? Away! The smell of leek makes me sick.

I peseech you heartily, scurfy, lousy knave, at my desires, / and my requests, and my petitions, to eat, look you, this / leek. Because, look you, you do not love it, nor your / affections and your appetites and your digestions doo's not / agree with it, I would desire you to eat it.

I beg you heartily, scurvy, lousy rogue, at my wish, my request and my petition, to eat, look you, this leek. Because, look you, you don't love it, and your tastes and your appetites and your digestion don't agree with it, I would like you to eat it.
Not for Cadwallader and all his goats.
Not for Cadwallader and all his goats.
There is one goat for you. [Strikes him] Will you be so / good, scald knave, as eat it?
There's one goat for you. (Hits him) Will you be so good, you scabby rogue, as to eat it?

You say very true, scald knave, when God's will is. I will / desire you to live in the mean time, and eat your victuals. / Come, there is sauce for it. [Strikes him] You call'd me / yesterday mountain-squire; but I will make you to-day a / squire of low degree. I pray you, fall to; if you can mock / a leek, you can eat a leek.

You say very true, scabby rogue, when God wills it. I'd like you to live in the meantime and eat your food. Come, here's some sauce for it. (Hits him) Yesterday you called me a mountain squire, but today I'll make you a squire of low degree. Please, tuck in; if you can mock a leek, you can eat a leek.
Enough, captain; you have astonish'd him.
I say, I will make him eat some part of my leek, or I will / peat his pate four days. Bite, I pray you; it is good for / your green wound and your ploody coxcomb.
I tell you, I'll make him eat some of my leek, or I'll beat his head for four days. Bite, please; it's good for your fresh wound and your bloody skull.
Yes, certainly, and out of doubt and out of question / too, and ambiguities.
Yes, certainly, and beyond doubt, and beyond question too, and ambiguities.
By this leek, I will most horribly revenge. I eat and / eat, I swear--
By this leek, I will take horrible revenge. I eat, and eat, I swear...
Eat, I pray you. Will you have some more sauce to / your leek? There is not enough leek to swear by.
Eat, please. Do you want more sauce with your leek? There's not enough leek to swear by.
Quiet thy cudgel; thou dost see I eat.
Keep your stick still; you can see I'm eating.

Much good do you, scald knave, heartily. Nay, pray you, / throw none away; the skin is good for your broken coxcomb. / When you take occasions to see leeks hereafter, I pray you, / mock at 'em; that is all.

May it do you much good, scabby rogue, heartily. No, please, don't throw any away; the skin is good for your broken head. When you get the chance to see leeks in future, please, mock them; that's all.
Ay, leeks is good. Hold you, there is a groat to heal / your pate.
Yes, leeks are good. Here, there's fourpence to heal your head.
Yes, verily and in truth you shall take it; or I have / another leek in my pocket, which you shall eat.
Yes, truly and indeed you shall take it; or I have another leek in my pocket, which you shall eat.
I take thy groat in earnest of revenge.
I take your fourpence as a down payment on revenge.
If I owe you anything I will pay you in cudgels. You / shall be a woodmonger, and buy nothing of me but cudgels. / God be wi' you, and keep you, and heal your pate.
If I owe you anything, I'll pay you in cudgels. You can be a timber merchant and buy nothing from me but cudgels. God be with you, and keep you, and heal your head.
All hell shall stir for this.
All hell will be stirred up for this.

Go, go; you are a counterfeit cowardly knave. Will you mock / at an ancient tradition, begun upon an honourable respect, and / worn as a memorable trophy of predeceased valour, and dare not / avouch in your deeds any of your words? I have seen you gleeking / and galling at this gentleman twice or thrice. You thought, / because he could not speak English in the native garb, he could / not therefore handle an English cudgel. You find it otherwise; / and henceforth let a Welsh correction teach you a good English / condition. Fare ye well.

Go on, go on; you're a fake, cowardly rogue. Will you mock an ancient tradition, begun for an honourable reason and worn as a memorable trophy of the courage of the dead, and not dare to back up any of your words with deeds? I've seen you jeering and taunting this gentleman two or three times. You thought, because he couldn't speak English the way natives do, he couldn't handle an English cudgel. You find otherwise; and from now on let a Welsh beating teach you good English manners. Farewell.
